w:r.w:t: Step 2 — The object the problem asks for: Euclidean fields, the axioms of Osterwalder and Schrader, and the reconstruction theorem
DATE: 1973–1975 (Osterwalder and Schrader). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

A Euclidean quantum field theory in d dimensions is given by its Schwinger functions S_n, n ≥ 1: continuous linear functionals on test functions of n points of ℝ^d. For the composite fields from which a gauge theory is built, the test functions vanish, with all their derivatives, wherever two points coincide. Let θ be the reflection x_d ↦ −x_d in the last coordinate (Euclidean time), let τ_v be the translation by v, and let 𝒮₊ consist of the test functions supported where every point has positive last coordinate. A finite family is a sequence f = (f₀, f₁, …, f_N) with f_n ∈ 𝒮₊(ℝ^{dn}); it stands for a polynomial in the smeared field, and for t ≥ 0 the correlation of the reflected, conjugated family with its translate is
S(θf̄ · τ_t f) = Σ_{n, n′} S_{n+n′}(θf̄_n ⊗ τ_t f_{n′}).

The axioms of Osterwalder and Schrader (Comm. Math. Phys. 31 (1973), 83–112; Comm. Math. Phys. 42 (1975), 281–305) are five. (E0) Regularity: each S_n is a distribution on its test space; the reconstruction theorem below uses the strengthened form (E0′) of the second paper, the linear growth condition, which bounds |S_n(f)| by one Schwartz seminorm of f of degree proportional to n with constants growing at most as a power of n!, and whose inequality is stated there in its exact form. (E1) Euclidean invariance: S_n(h·f) = S_n(f) for every Euclidean motion h of ℝ^d. (E2) Reflection positivity: S(θf̄ · f) ≥ 0 for every finite family f. (E3) Symmetry: each S_n is invariant under permutations of its arguments. (E4) Cluster property: for finite families f, g and every spatial vector v ≠ 0, S(θf̄ · τ_{sv} g) → S(θf̄) S(g) as s → ∞.

Theorem (Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction). Schwinger functions satisfying (E0) in its strengthened form and (E1)–(E3) determine a Hilbert space ℋ, a unit vector Ω, a positive self-adjoint Hamiltonian H with HΩ = 0, a unitary representation of the Poincaré group and Wightman fields, from which the S_n are recovered by analytic continuation. Each finite family f defines a vector [f] ∈ ℋ; these vectors are dense in ℋ, ⟨Ω, [f]⟩ = S(f), and for t ≥ 0
Given (E0)–(E3), the cluster property (E4) holds exactly when Ω is, up to a phase, the only vector invariant under the translations.
The explanation

Reflection positivity is the axiom that manufactures the Hilbert space. On the finite families supported at positive time the form ⟨f, g⟩ := S(θf̄ · g) is a positive semidefinite sesquilinear form by (E2); the quotient by its null vectors, completed, is ℋ, and the class of the empty family is the vacuum Ω. Translation in time by t ≥ 0 maps 𝒮₊ into itself and is a contraction for this form by (E1) and (E2) together, and the contractions e^{−tH} so obtained form a strongly continuous self-adjoint semigroup; its generator H is positive and self-adjoint, and HΩ = 0 because the empty family is fixed by every translation. Spatial translations and the remaining Euclidean motions give the unitary representation; the analytic continuation of the Schwinger functions in the time differences, which (E0) in its strengthened form guarantees, gives the Wightman functions and the Wightman fields (Glimm and Jaffe, Quantum Physics: A Functional Integral Point of View, second edition, 1987, Chapter 6). The mass gap of the conclusion is a property of exactly this H: the problem is a statement about the spectrum of the operator that reflection positivity constructs, and nothing about any other operator.
Consistency

Uses Step 1. The Hilbert space ℋ, the vacuum Ω and the Hamiltonian H named here are the ℋ, Ω and H of the conclusion's spectral condition. Every later step that constructs Schwinger functions on a lattice and passes to a limit is measured against (E0)–(E4) as stated here, and the lattice form of this theorem is Step 4.
Step 3 — Wilson's lattice gauge theory
DATE: 1974 (Wilson). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Let G be a compact Lie group, G = SU(N) in what follows, and let Λ be the periodic lattice of spacing a and side L in d = 4 dimensions. To each oriented bond b of Λ is assigned a group element U_b ∈ G with U_{−b} = U_b^{−1}, and to each plaquette p (an elementary square of the lattice, with an orientation) the ordered product U_p of the four bond variables around it. Wilson's measure (K. G. Wilson, "Confinement of quarks", Phys. Rev. D 10 (1974), 2445–2459) is
dμ_β(U) = Z^{−1} exp( −β Σ_p ( 1 − (1/N) Re tr U_p ) ) Π_b dU_b,

with dU_b the normalised Haar measure of G on each bond and Z the normalising constant. It is invariant under the gauge transformations U_{xy} ↦ g_x U_{xy} g_y^{−1}, g : Λ → G, and the observables of the theory are the gauge-invariant functions of the bond variables. For SU(2) the plaquette energy a_p(U) = 1 − ½ tr U_p ∈ [0, 2] is the gauge-invariant scalar whose smeared and centred sums are the theory's basic observable, the lattice form of the action density tr F².
The explanation

Gauge invariance is a change of variables: the Haar measure is invariant under left and right multiplication, each plaquette product transforms as U_p ↦ g_x U_p g_x^{−1} at its base point x, and the trace is a class function, so the exponent is unchanged. Because G is compact and the Haar measure is a probability measure, dμ_β is a probability measure on the compact space G^{bonds} for every β ≥ 0 with no gauge fixing: the lattice theory is a well-defined measure at every coupling, which is why the lattice is the setting of every construction that follows. With U_{x,μ} = exp(i a g A_μ(x)) for a smooth connection A and β = 2N/g², the exponent is a Riemann sum of the Yang–Mills action ¼ ∫ F^a_{μν} F^a_{μν} d⁴x as a → 0, which is the sense in which Wilson's theory is the lattice form of Yang–Mills theory. The correlations of the plaquette energy at distinct sites are Schwinger functions of a composite field, the lattice forms of the S_n of Step 2 for the field tr F².
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–2. Every lattice quantity in this document — a gap, a clustering rate, a coupling — is a quantity of this measure dμ_β or of its blocked and effective descendants, and every group G of the conclusion enters through this definition.
Step 4 — Reflection positivity, the transfer matrix and the lattice gap
DATE: 1912 (Jentzsch); 1977 (Lüscher); 1978 (Osterwalder and Seiler); the kernel form of the finite gap 2026-10-27. STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Theorem (Osterwalder and Seiler, "Gauge field theories on a lattice", Ann. Physics 110 (1978), 440–471). Wilson's measure is reflection positive: if ϑ is the reflection of Λ in a lattice hyperplane orthogonal to a coordinate axis and F is a function of the bond variables on one side of it, then ∫ ϑF̄ · F dμ_β ≥ 0.

Theorem (Lüscher, "Construction of a selfadjoint, strictly positive transfer matrix for Euclidean lattice gauge theories", Comm. Math. Phys. 54 (1977), 283–292). For Wilson's action there is a self-adjoint, strictly positive transfer matrix T acting on the gauge-invariant functions of the bond variables of one time slice, such that time-ordered correlations on a torus of time extent Na are traces of products of T with the observables. On a torus of finite spatial volume T is an integral operator with a continuous, strictly positive kernel on a compact space.

Theorem (Jentzsch, "Über Integralgleichungen mit positivem Kern", J. Reine Angew. Math. 141 (1912), 235–244). An integral operator with a continuous, strictly positive kernel on a compact space has a largest eigenvalue λ₀ that is simple, with a strictly positive eigenfunction ψ₀, and every other eigenvalue is strictly smaller in modulus.
Definition (the lattice gap). Let λ₁ be the largest eigenvalue of T below λ₀ on the gauge-invariant sector. The lattice mass gap is
m_lat = log(λ₀/λ₁)

in units of the lattice spacing; its value in physical units is m_lat/a. In the state defined by ψ₀, which is the limit of infinite time extent at fixed spatial volume, an observable A of the bond variables at positive times defines, by integration over the half-lattice with A inserted, a vector Φ_A on the time slice, and for every number n of time steps
⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ = ⟨Φ_A, (T/λ₀)^n Φ_A⟩.

The finite form of the definition is a theorem of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step: for an entrywise-positive symmetric matrix T on a finite cross-section, every eigenvalue λ_i other than the Perron root λ₀ satisfies λ₀ − |λ_i| > 0, and in energies log λ₀ − log |λ_i| > 0 whenever λ_i ≠ 0 (theorems finite_volume_mass_gap and finite_volume_mass_gap_log of the file Aperanton/MassGap.lean; the Perron root's simplicity and strict dominance for such matrices, the finite-dimensional form of Jentzsch's theorem, in Aperanton/Perron.lean, which is Perron's theorem of 1907 and Frobenius's of 1912).
The explanation

Reflection positivity makes the lattice theory a quantum mechanics: it is the lattice form of axiom (E2), and the construction of Step 2 applied to it gives the Hilbert space of gauge-invariant functions of one time slice on which T acts, with T/λ₀ playing the part of e^{−aH} for one unit of Euclidean time. The problem statement calls this positivity "a major advantage" and adds that "establishing a quantum mechanical Hilbert space is part of the solution to this Millennium problem" (Jaffe and Witten, the official problem description, §6.5). Jentzsch's theorem is what makes the vacuum unique on every finite spatial volume at every coupling: the kernel of T is a product of Boltzmann factors of a bounded action, hence strictly positive and continuous on the compact group manifold of the slice's bond variables, so λ₀ is simple and every other eigenvalue is strictly smaller. The lattice gap is therefore strictly positive on every finite cross-section at every coupling; the content of the problem is that this gap, divided by the spacing, stays bounded below as the volume grows and the spacing shrinks along the sequence of couplings fixed by asymptotic freedom.
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–3. The identity ⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ = ⟨Φ_A, (T/λ₀)^n Φ_A⟩ is the lattice form of Step 2's ⟨[f], e^{−tH}[f]⟩ = S(θf̄ · τ_t f). The gap m_lat defined here is the quantity every later lattice bound concerns, and m_lat/a is what must stay bounded below for the conclusion's Δ.
Step 5 — The gap governs reflection-positive decay
DATE: 2026-10-27 (the kernel form) and 2026-10-28 (the lemma). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics
Lemma. Let q = λ₁/λ₀. For every gauge-invariant observable A at positive times and every n ≥ 0,
0 ≤ ⟨ϑĀ · τ_n A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² ≤ q^n ( ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² ).

Proof. Write Φ_A = ⟨ψ₀, Φ_A⟩ψ₀ + φ with φ ⊥ ψ₀. Since ⟨ψ₀, Φ_A⟩ = ⟨A⟩₀ and ψ₀ is fixed by T/λ₀, the middle term equals ⟨φ, (T/λ₀)^n φ⟩. The operator T/λ₀ is positive, and on the orthogonal complement of ψ₀ its norm is q. Hence 0 ≤ ⟨φ, (T/λ₀)^n φ⟩ ≤ q^n ‖φ‖², and ‖φ‖² = ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|² is the case n = 0. ∎

The finite form of the lemma is a theorem of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step (theorem twopoint_le_of_gap of the file Aperanton/Scaling.lean): for a positive semidefinite matrix M with strictly positive entries, a number q ≥ 0 such that every eigenvalue other than the Perron root λ₀ is at most q λ₀, any real vector f and any R ≥ 0, there is a Perron eigenvector Ω of M with every entry nonzero such that
0 ≤ f · (M^R f) / λ₀^R − (Ω · f)² ≤ (f · f) q^R.

Its proof in the kernel is the moment representation: f · (M^R f) = Σ_k m_k λ_k^R with m_k ≥ 0 the squared components of f along an orthonormal eigenbasis, Σ_k m_k = f · f, the Perron term m_{k₀} λ₀^R = (Ω · f)² λ₀^R removed, and every other term bounded by m_k (q λ₀)^R.
The explanation

The lemma is the spectral theorem applied once: a gap in the spectrum of the transfer matrix forces every connected reflection-positive two-point function to decay at least geometrically in the time separation, at the rate q = e^{−m_lat}, and to be nonnegative. Two features of the bound carry the later steps. The constant on the right, ⟨ϑĀ · A⟩₀ − |⟨A⟩₀|², is a correlation between A and its mirror image, whose supports are separated by twice the distance of A from the reflection plane; it is therefore controlled by bounds on correlations at separated points, which is the only kind of bound a construction of a composite field can provide. And on a torus of finite time extent N the correlations differ from those of the state ψ₀ by terms bounded, at a fixed lattice, by multiples of q^{N−n} and of tr(T/λ₀)^N − 1, which tend to zero as the time extent grows at fixed spatial volume; the kernel's theorem mass_gap_rate of the same development gives the residual bound |tr(T^L) − λ₀^L| ≤ (dim − 1)(ρλ₀)^L with ρ < 1 that controls the second term.
Consistency

Uses Steps 1–4; q is Step 4's λ₁/λ₀ and ψ₀, Φ_A are Step 4's. The inequality is used, in the direction gap ⇒ decay, by every later step that turns a lattice gap into exponential clustering, and its converse, decay ⇒ gap, is the content of the equivalence proved later for reflection-positive theories.
Step 6 — Bałaban's renormalisation group: the scaling sequence, the coarse scale, the blocks, the block map, the blocked measure and the fibre
DATE: 1985–1989 (Bałaban); the definitions in this form 2026-10-28. STATUS: DEFINITIONS, the framework on which the ultraviolet half and the reduction of the later steps rest.
The mathematics

A continuum limit requires bounds on the lattice theory that are uniform as the spacing tends to zero along a sequence of bare couplings tuned by asymptotic freedom. Bałaban's renormalisation group provides such bounds on a torus: it integrates out the fluctuations of one length scale after another, each step followed by a rescaling, chooses gauges that vary from cell to cell and from scale to scale, and controls the effective actions uniformly in the spacing, with an analysis of asymptotic freedom and of the regions of large field — in three dimensions unconditionally, in four dimensions under the hypothesis that the running couplings stay below a constant at every scale (T. Bałaban, "Ultraviolet stability of three-dimensional lattice pure gauge field theories", Comm. Math. Phys. 102 (1985), 255–275; "Renormalization group approach to lattice gauge field theories. I", Comm. Math. Phys. 109 (1987), 249–301; "Large field renormalization. II. Localization, exponentiation, and bounds for the R operation", Comm. Math. Phys. 122 (1989), 355–392; and the further papers of the series in Comm. Math. Phys. 99 (1985), 116 (1988) and 119 (1988)).

The scaling sequence and the coarse scale. The construction uses Wilson measures μ_j on periodic lattices of spacings a_j = a₀ L^{−K_j}, with L a fixed integer and K_j → ∞, whose sides tend to infinity, with bare couplings tuned along the sequence; j is the rung. Fix a physical length a_c = L^{k₀} a₀ with k₀ ≥ 0, the coarse scale, and take lattices whose sides are multiples of a_c, the time extent an even multiple when L is odd, so that the half period lies on the lattice, and whose reflection hyperplane is one of the hyperplanes x₀ = n a_c. Every spacing a_j then divides a_c; the half-open cubes of side a_c with corners on the coarse lattice ℤ⁴ of spacing a_c, reduced modulo the sides, partition the lattice of rung j into blocks, each link assigned to the block containing its midpoint. B_y is the block at the coarse point y, and |y − y′| = max_ν |y_ν − y′_ν| the distance on the coarse lattice; the four links of a plaquette lie in blocks at mutual distance at most one. For a bounded observable f, a function of the links, S(f) is the set of blocks containing a link on which f depends, N(f) its cardinality, ‖f‖ its supremum norm, and δ_y(f) the oscillation of f under changes of the links of B_y alone, so that δ_y(f) ≤ 2‖f‖ and δ_y(f) = 0 off S(f); the distance between two sets of blocks is the least distance between their members. For a smeared Wilson loop, for a polynomial in such loops, and for every observable whose support and bound are fixed in physical units, N(f) and ‖f‖ are bounded uniformly in j.

The block map. A block map is a measurable bijection of the configurations of a block onto a product V × Φ_j, with measurable inverse, the same for every block, in which V is a fixed compact space, the space of the coarse variables, and Φ_j is compact, the space of the fine coordinates. Two maps are used. The holonomy map assigns one SU(2) element per coarse link, the holonomy of the block along a fixed path with the remaining links in a fixed gauge. The block average assigns to each coarse link the average over the n³ parallel fine paths of its block, n = a_c/a_j, extended measurably to the configurations at which the average vanishes; the averaged variables of Bałaban's renormalisation group, on blocks of odd side centred on the coarse points, are of this kind. Write v_y ∈ V and φ_y ∈ Φ_j for the coordinates of the links of B_y. The blocked measure λ_j is the law of the coarse configuration v = (v_y) under μ_j, and the fibre measure ν_j(· | v) is the conditional law of the fine coordinates φ = (φ_y) given v: the Gibbs measure on the fibres whose conditional at a block is the Wilson conditional of that block restricted to its fibre, defined for every v. The blocked measure has conditional laws λ_j(dv_y | v) given the other coarse variables, and Dobrushin's interdependence matrix of the blocked measure is
C^λ_j(y, y′) = sup ‖λ_j(· | v) − λ_j(· | v′)‖_TV,

the supremum over pairs v, v′ of coarse configurations that differ only at y′, and ‖·‖_TV the total variation distance of the two conditional laws of v_y. The coarse variables are of one type at every rung, so the total variation is taken on one fixed space for every j. The coarse coordinate of a block is a function of that block's links alone, and a change of it at fixed fine coordinates changes the links of that block alone; so a change of one coarse variable alters the Wilson conditionals at that block and at the blocks adjacent to it, and nowhere else.
The explanation

The coarse scale is a fixed physical length: as j grows the blocks hold more and more fine links, but the coarse lattice, its distance and the space V of the coarse variables never change, which is what lets a statement about one block carry constants independent of the cutoff. The choice of block map is not a formality. For the Gaussian field with covariance g²(−Δ)^{−1} in Feynman gauge, the flux through an n × n square, the angle of the coarse plaquette the holonomy map defines, has variance g²(4G₃(0) n + o(n)), where 4G₃(0) = 4 Σ_{m∈ℤ} G₄(m e₁) = 2W/3, G_d is the inverse of the d-dimensional lattice Laplacian and W = √6 Γ(1/24)Γ(5/24)Γ(7/24)Γ(11/24)/(32π³) is the return sum of the three-dimensional walk: the variance is g² times the sum of G₄ over pairs of boundary links of the square weighted by their orientations, perpendicular sides do not couple, each side with itself gives S_n = Σ_{|m|<n} (n − |m|) G₄(m e₁), the opposite sides give −T_n with 0 ≤ T_n ≤ n G₃(n e₂), which is bounded, and S_n/n → G₃(0) by dominated convergence, G₄(m e₁) being summable. Along the asymptotically free sequence, where g² falls only as 1/log n, this variance diverges, so at one loop every character mean of the path holonomy tends to zero, its coarse variables tend to independent Haar variables, and a reduction through them reduces nothing. The block average is free of this: in the same Gaussian field the flux of its coarse plaquette has variance converging, as n → ∞, to g² times the finite integral 2 ∫ |Π_ν φ(q_ν)|² |1 − e^{iq₂}|² |q|^{−2} d⁴q/(2π)⁴, with φ(q) = (e^{iq} − 1)/(iq), the integrand dominated by an integrable function on ℝ⁴; along the sequence it falls like 1/log n, a weak-coupling variable, as the coarse variables of Bałaban's renormalisation group are. For the block average the Gaussian part of the fibre is exact: given the block averages, the conditional covariance of the free field on ℤ⁴, at any mass and in any dimension, decays between blocks at a rate whose exact value is cosh κ_n = 2 + 3/(n² − 1) per coarse unit, so that κ_n decreases to log(2 + √3) = 1.3170 as n → ∞ and the rate per coarse unit is at least that number at every level, with a constant independent of the cutoff; for the holonomy map the same fibre carries the long modes and its rate falls like n^{−1/2}. The coarse variables of the ultraviolet analysis are therefore the block averages, and the reduction of the later steps is read for them.
Consistency

Uses Steps 3–5: μ_j is Step 3's measure at rung j, its transfer matrix and gap are Step 4's, and the reflection hyperplanes x₀ = n a_c are the hyperplanes of Step 4's positivity. The spacings a_j → 0 are the continuum limit of the conclusion; the hypotheses on the blocked measure and the fibre, and the theorem that turns them into the gap, are later steps in exactly these terms.
Step 7 — The existence constructions in the literature, and the one property each leaves open
DATE: 6 October 2026 to 29 October 2026 (the documents, read at their primary sources). STATUS: A READING OF THE RECORD; every clause is the cited document's own statement.
The mathematics

Three dimensions. The manuscript YMM1 of L. Alpöge and E. Sussman, "Scalar fields from three-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills theory" (the authors' public repository at its commit of 27 October 2026; 854 pages, a revised edition of 856), studies the scalar observable 𝒪_K(f) = a_K^{−1} Σ_p f(x(p)) a_p on the lattices a_K ℤ³, a_K = L^{−K}, L ≥ 13 odd, the sum over the positive plaquettes of all three orientations, x(p) the barycentre and a_p = 1 − ½ tr U_p the plaquette energy of Step 3, centred by its expectation. Its Theorem A asserts, on a fixed torus of side 2L^m, that the connected correlations of the smeared densities converge along the full sequence of lattices. Its Theorem B passes to infinite volume along a subsequence, the limit having zero one-point function, invariance under all Euclidean isometries and reflection positivity at every plane, and carrying a canonical component measure (X, λ, (σ_ξ)) with σ = ∫ σ_ξ dλ(ξ), each component obeying

uniformly in ξ; the manuscript states that "the infinite-volume conclusion is subsequential" and that the fixed-torus estimate "does not give uniqueness of these infinite-volume limits". Its Theorem 0 asserts, along K = K_j, limits satisfying (E0) with the explicit bound |S_n(φ)| ≤ 2C^n (n!)^8 |φ|_{8n} together with (E1)–(E4), reconstructing in one of the canonical clustering components a Hermitian scalar Wightman field with a unique invariant vacuum; of the original limit it says that "vacuum uniqueness and clustering are not asserted" and that its zero-energy space is L²(X, λ). Its Theorem C is the short-distance law κ₂(f, h) = (9/(16π²)) b^{−2} 𝒦_free(f, h)(1 + e), 𝒦_free(f, h) = ∬ f(x)h(y)|x − y|^{−6} dx dy, |e| ≤ ε(d) → 0 as d → 0, the kernel being the two-point function of the free action density in three dimensions. The manuscript closes its statement of Theorem B with the sentence that "the construction makes no identification with a tensor-valued field strength and asserts no mass gap".

Four dimensions. The same authors' draft "SU(2) Yang–Mills theory in four dimensions via Balaban's renormalisation group: construction, axioms and non-triviality" (6 October 2026, 153 pages) is conditional from its first sentence, "assuming the proof inputs declared clause by clause in Section 9". Under them it deduces: the running coupling exists at every scale with two-sided linear flow bounds uniform in the cutoff and the exact one-loop law for SU(2) at small coupling; Bałaban's ultraviolet stability theorem; connected correlations of smeared action densities bounded uniformly in the cutoff; limits on each torus without subsequences and on ℝ⁴ along subsequences of cutoffs and volumes, satisfying (E0) in a stated form, invariance under translations and the hypercubic group, (E2) and (E3), whence a Hilbert space with a vacuum and a non-negative Hamiltonian; a two-point law in the running coupling uniform in the volume; and invariance under O(4) under a hypothesis on the flux of the lattice rotation current through far spheres. It states what it does not claim: "uniqueness of the infinite-volume limit (the limits on ℝ⁴ are taken along subsequences of volumes), uniqueness of the vacuum, the cluster property, a mass gap, the growth condition of [22] in the number of points (hence field operators or Wightman functions), anything at coinciding points, invariance under all rotations without the hypothesis of clause (vi), statements about Wilson loops or about Balaban's block-averaged variables, or any statement for SU(N), N ≥ 3"; its Remark 4.19 gives the reason: "The constants in our bounds do not decay as the separation of the supports grows, so no decay of the connected functions is available." Two of its supporting statements are not yet written, and its authors state that all claims of the repository are to be understood as tentative, pending verification.

The other claims in public view on 29 October 2026, each read at the place where its gap is obtained. An announcement by OpenAI of 26 October 2026 of a rigorous existence proof in four dimensions, 1,147 pages, unreleased, with a review group whose statement says that Bałaban's ideas "enabled OpenAI to follow the theory all the way to infinite distances and prove the existence of its proper continuum limit. But confinement and the mass gap remain very important open challenges" (the sentences as reproduced by P. Woit, Not Even Wrong, the post of 26 October 2026). M. Faizal and A. Shabir, "Reflection-Positive Construction of a Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang–Mills Theory with Mass Gap and Confinement", arXiv:2606.19362, Fortschritte der Physik 74 (2026), e70097: the persistence of the gap across scales, its Theorem 5.6, assumes the interlacing inequality γ_{k+1} ≥ γ_k − δ_k with Σ δ_k < ∞, and the summability, its Proposition 5.5, holds under locality hypotheses that guarantee |U_k(X)| ≤ C e^{−c ℓ} for every connected Ursell kernel of diameter ℓ at every scale — exponential clustering at every scale is its hypothesis; its Theorem 9.4 identifies two constructions "if μ_k = μ̃_k and K_k = K̃_k on a core of local observables", so its Theorem 10.8 presupposes the identification it asserts. R. Fontes, Zenodo record 18969699 (11 March 2026): the decay at its minimum coupling β₀ = 9587 is asserted by a cluster expansion inside one block of side two with its boundary fixed, the manuscript itself noting that at β = 9587 "no RG step is needed"; its mechanism is group-blind and would give the four-dimensional U(1) theory a gap at weak coupling, which the theorems of Guth and of Fröhlich and Spencer exclude; and three of its one-block constants are wrong, the least eigenvalue of the full 120-plaquette Hessian of a block of side two being 3, not the 0.6893 of its 72-plaquette truncation (the full Hessian is facesᵀfaces + 3I with spectrum 3, 7, 9, 11 of multiplicities 15, 6, 8, 3, exactly), its entropy inequality failing for animals of four plaquettes, and its Peierls condition at θ = 0.025 assuming the probability 0.0500 where the one-plaquette law at β = 9587 gives 0.1118. B. Lee, Zenodo record 19601454 (16 April 2026): the gap m₀ ≥ ρ₀ follows from its Assumption 2.1, a logarithmic Sobolev floor uniform in the spacing, carried by a relative-entropy bound KL(μ₀ ‖ μ) ≤ M held fixed by choice, whereas for a Gibbs measure that relative entropy grows with the volume and as the spacing tends to zero. A GitHub repository announcing a resolution for SU(3) (16 to 28 October 2026): its master theorem is stated under a continuum bridge and a non-perturbative cluster decay, its gap 1.552 ± 0.038 GeV enters by insertion, and its polymer contraction is evaluated at the finest scale only and asserted uniform toward the infrared. Zenodo record 23001803 (27 September 2026): a spectral gap for the SU(2) Kogut–Susskind Hamiltonian on open spatial boxes at strong coupling, uniform in the box and the spacing, for g² ≥ 3.978 unconditionally, which states its own limit — the continuum path leaves its domain after finitely many steps — and claims no crossing.
The explanation

Measured against the problem statement, the constructions supply, under their declared inputs, the existence of limits along subsequences with the axioms (E0)–(E3), non-triviality by a short-distance law, and in three dimensions clustering with an inverse first power of the separation in the components of the limit; none supplies a mass gap, and the claims of a gap rest in every case on the gap itself, assumed at every scale or inserted as a number. The problem statement's second footnote excludes a limit by compactness "unless one also uses other techniques to establish properties of the limit (such as the existence of a mass gap and the axioms)", so a limit so obtained establishes the existence part only together with a proof of those properties for the limit obtained. Step 8 — The gap is exponential clustering
DATE: 2026-10-28 (the identification; its kernel form 2026-10-27). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Let S be reflection positive and invariant under time translations, and let ℋ, Ω and H ≥ 0 be the Hilbert space, the vacuum and the Hamiltonian that the construction of Step 2 gives from these two properties, with the relations ⟨Ω, [f]⟩ = S(f) and ⟨[f], e^{−tH}[f]⟩ = S(θf̄ · τ_t f) for t ≥ 0.

Theorem. Let m > 0. The following are equivalent. (a) Ω is, up to a phase, the only vector annihilated by H, and H has no spectrum in the interval (0, m). (b) For every finite family f and every t ≥ 0, S(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S(f)|² ≤ e^{−mt}(S(θf̄ · f) − |S(f)|²). (c) For every finite family f there are a constant C_f and an unbounded set T_f ⊂ [0, ∞) such that S(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S(f)|² ≤ C_f e^{−mt} for every t ∈ T_f. When they hold and ℋ has dimension at least two, the mass m* = inf spec(H restricted to Ω^⊥) satisfies m ≤ m* < ∞.
Proof. For a finite family f put ψ_f = [f] − S(f)Ω. Since ⟨Ω, [f]⟩ = S(f), the vector ψ_f is the orthogonal projection of [f] onto Ω^⊥, and since e^{−tH}Ω = Ω,
⟨ψ_f, e^{−tH} ψ_f⟩ = S(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S(f)|², t ≥ 0.

The space Ω^⊥ reduces H, and since the vectors [f] are dense in ℋ, the vectors ψ_f are dense in Ω^⊥. (a) ⇒ (b): by (a) the restriction of H to Ω^⊥ has spectrum in [m, ∞), so e^{−tH} ≤ e^{−mt} on Ω^⊥ by the spectral theorem; apply this to ψ_f in the identity, whose case t = 0 identifies ‖ψ_f‖². (b) ⇒ (c): take C_f = S(θf̄ · f) − |S(f)|² and T_f = [0, ∞). (c) ⇒ (a): let μ_f be the spectral measure of H in the vector ψ_f, a finite positive measure on [0, ∞). For 0 ≤ m′ < m and t ∈ T_f the identity and (c) give

so μ_f([0, m′]) ≤ C_f e^{−(m−m′)t} for arbitrarily large t, and μ_f([0, m′]) = 0. Letting m′ increase to m gives μ_f([0, m)) = 0, which says that Eψ_f = 0 for the spectral projection E of H onto [0, m). The ψ_f are dense in Ω^⊥ and E is bounded, so E vanishes on Ω^⊥. Hence H ≥ m on Ω^⊥: no nonzero vector of Ω^⊥ is annihilated by H, and H has no spectrum in (0, m), which is (a). Finally, if dim ℋ ≥ 2 then Ω^⊥ ≠ {0}, the spectrum of H on Ω^⊥ is a nonempty closed subset of [m, ∞), and its infimum m* is finite. ∎

Corollary (clustering). Under the conditions of the theorem, for all finite families f and g and every t ≥ 0, |S(θḡ · τ_t f) − S(θḡ) S(f)| ≤ e^{−mt} ‖ψ_g‖ ‖ψ_f‖. If S also satisfies (E0)–(E3), the cluster property (E4) holds, and the same bound holds with τ_t replaced by the translation by t in any direction. Proof. The left side is |⟨ψ_g, e^{−tH} ψ_f⟩|, and e^{−tH} has norm at most e^{−mt} on Ω^⊥. Under (E0)–(E3) the vacuum is unique by the theorem, and the reconstruction theorem of Step 2 gives (E4). A translation in another direction is conjugate to τ_t by a Euclidean rotation, under which S is invariant by (E1), and the reflection Hilbert space built across the rotated hyperplane carries the same Hamiltonian spectrum, since the Schwinger functions it is built from are the same functions. ∎

The finite form of the implication (c) ⇒ (a), the gap read off the decay of a positive symmetric transfer matrix, is a theorem of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step (theorems eigenvalue_le_of_decay and gap_of_decay of the file Aperanton/Decay.lean): for a positive semidefinite matrix M with strictly positive entries, a Perron eigenvector Ω, and a number α ≥ 0 such that for every vector f there is a K with |f · (M^R f)/λ₀^R − (Ω · f)²| ≤ K α^R for every R, every eigenvalue λ_k other than the Perron root satisfies λ_k ≤ α λ₀; and for 0 < α and every positive such eigenvalue, log λ₀ − log λ_k ≥ −log α.
The explanation

The argument is the spectral theorem applied to the semigroup e^{−tH}; its weight lies in the identification it makes. A mass gap is a statement about the spectrum of an operator that only reflection positivity constructs, and exponential decay of the reflection-positive correlations is a statement about numbers a lattice computation can bound; the theorem says that for a reflection-positive theory these are one and the same property, with the same m. Condition (c) is the form a construction can verify: a bound along an unbounded set of times, with constants that may depend on the observable. The problem statement's own remark that clustering is "an important consequence of the existence of a mass gap" is here made exact and reversed: the clustering is also sufficient.

Step 9 — The completion: uniform exponential clustering on the lattice gives every limit point the gap, the unique vacuum and the cluster property
DATE: 2026-10-28 (the theorem; its kernel forms 2026-10-27). STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Lemma (passage to the limit). Let S_j be Schwinger functions converging to S, along a subsequence, on the test functions flat at the coincidence diagonals, and let D ⊂ [0, ∞) be unbounded. Suppose that for every finite family f there are a constant C_f and numbers r_j(t; f), with r_j(t; f) → 0 as j → ∞ for each t ∈ D, such that S_j(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S_j(f)|² ≤ C_f e^{−mt} + r_j(t; f) for t ∈ D. Then S satisfies condition (c) of Step 8. Proof. For a finite family f and t ≥ 0 the families θf̄ and τ_t f are supported in opposite half-spaces, so every test function entering S_j(θf̄ · τ_t f) is flat at the coincidence diagonals, and both sides of the hypothesis converge along the subsequence. The inequality passes to the limit, with T_f = D. ∎

Theorem (the completion). Let a construction be given by Wilson measures on periodic lattices of spacings a_j = a₀ L^{−K_j}, with L a fixed integer and K_j → ∞, whose sides tend to infinity, with bare couplings tuned along the sequence; and let the Schwinger functions S_j of smeared gauge-invariant observables converge along a subsequence to S. Let D be the set of times n a₀ L^{−k} with n, k ≥ 0. Suppose that the lattice correlations cluster uniformly at a physical rate m > 0: for every finite family f there are a constant C_f and numbers r_j(t; f) → 0 as j → ∞ for each t ∈ D, such that
S_j(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S_j(f)|² ≤ C_f e^{−mt} + r_j(t; f) for t ∈ D.

Then S has a unique vacuum, its Hamiltonian has no spectrum in (0, m), and its connected reflection-positive correlations decay in time at the rate m. If S is non-trivial, its mass is finite. The hypothesis holds, with r_j = 0, when the S_j are the correlations of the states ψ₀ of spatial tori, the transfer matrices satisfy m_lat(j) ≥ m a_j on the sector generated by the observables, and the correlations at separated points are bounded uniformly in j.

Proof. The set D is unbounded and independent of f. The lemma gives condition (c) of Step 8 for S, and Step 8's theorem with its corollary gives the conclusions; non-triviality means that ℋ has dimension at least two. For the last sentence, each t ∈ D is an integer multiple n_j a_j of the spacing for all large j, and the smeared observable of τ_t f is then the lattice translate by n_j steps of the smeared observable of f. With q_j = λ₁/λ₀ for the transfer matrix of rung j, so that −log q_j = m_lat(j) ≥ m a_j, Step 5's lemma gives S_j(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S_j(f)|² ≤ q_j^{n_j}(S_j(θf̄ · f) − |S_j(f)|²) ≤ e^{−mt}(S_j(θf̄ · f) − |S_j(f)|²), and the bracket is a correlation at separated points, bounded uniformly in j by a constant depending only on f. ∎

Corollary (what the gap supplies against the footnote). For a construction by compactness of the kind in the theorem, uniform clustering at a physical rate, and in particular a lattice gap uniform in physical units, supplies the mass gap and the uniqueness of the vacuum. With (E0)–(E3), (E1) meaning full Euclidean invariance, it supplies the properties that the problem statement's footnote names: the mass gap and the axioms. Proof. The theorem gives the gap and the unique vacuum; with (E0)–(E3), Step 8's corollary gives the cluster property (E4), which completes the axioms. ∎

Corollary (the gap collapses the component measure). If the original limit σ of Theorem B of the three-dimensional manuscript of Step 7 satisfies condition (c) of Step 8, then its component measure λ is a point mass, σ is itself a clustering theory, and its connected correlations decay exponentially in every direction. Proof. By that Theorem B the zero-energy space of σ is L²(X, λ), with the vacuum the constant 1. By Step 8 the zero-energy space is spanned by Ω, so L²(X, λ) is one-dimensional. If λ were not a point mass, a Borel set B with 0 < λ(B) < 1 would give a function 1_B independent of 1 in L²(X, λ). Hence λ is a point mass; since λ has full support, X is a single point and σ = σ_ξ. The decay is exponential in time by Step 8's corollary and in every direction by the Euclidean invariance of σ. ∎

The finite forms are theorems of the Lean 4 kernel above the Mathlib library, with no unproved step (the file Aperanton/Scaling.lean): a scaling sequence is a sequence of spacings a_n > 0 tending to zero with their couplings, the physical gap along it the lower bound Δ ≤ Δ_lat(n)/a_n at every n; a family of lattice two-point functions C(n, R) with |C(n, R)| ≤ K e^{−Δ_lat(n) R} clusters uniformly in physical distance, |C(n, R)| ≤ K e^{−Δ a_n R} (theorem clustersUniformly_of_gap); and the gap passes to the limit: if such a family converges, at every physical separation x along the lattice points nearest to it, to a limit function, that limit is at most K e^{−Δ x} (theorem cluster_of_limit). The theorem turns the whole problem into two finite kinds of reading at every rung: a lattice gap in physical units, m_lat(j) ≥ m a_j, and bounds on correlations at separated points, which are what a construction of a composite field provides. It does not require the limit to be unique, and it claims nothing about the limit's existence, which the constructions of Step 7 supply along subsequences under their declared inputs; it asserts that whatever limit is obtained, if the lattice gap stayed bounded below in physical units along the sequence, has the gap, the unique vacuum and the cluster property. The object. The object that remains is the infinite-volume mass gap of the four-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills theory at every coupling, uniform in physical units along the scaling sequence of Step 6: a constant m > 0 with

The sharp one-link lemma. Read each element of SU(2) as a unit vector of ℝ⁴. The conditional law of one link U given the other links is the heat-bath kernel: with w = β times the sum of the six staples of the link (the staple of a plaquette being the product of its other three links, read as a unit vector), it is the law ν_w on the unit sphere S³ whose density with respect to the uniform measure is proportional to e^{⟨u, w⟩}, the von Mises–Fisher law. This law moves in total variation by at most 2β/(3π) times the change of the staple sum: because the mean absolute deviation of a coordinate ⟨u, e⟩ of ν_w, for every unit vector e and every w, is at most 4/(3π), its value at the uniform law, with equality there alone; and the derivative of ν_w along a segment from w to w′ is bounded by that deviation, every law along the segment being a von Mises–Fisher law, so the total variation along the segment is at most (2/(3π))|w − w′|. A neighbouring link's change moves the staple sum by at most 2 in norm, and each link of ℤ⁴ has eighteen neighbouring links (six plaquettes, three other links each), so Dobrushin's single-site condition, the row sum 18 · 4β/(3π) < 1, holds on the full lattice for

and in the temporal gauge on lattices open in time, where every time link is the identity and a space link has fourteen neighbouring links rather than eighteen — four spatial plaquettes with three other space links each and two temporal plaquettes with one — for β < 3π/56 = 0.1683. The bound on the mean absolute deviation is certified by an enclosure of 9,104 rectangles in the plane of the two parameters of the law, no cell undecided, with the axial case by Chebyshev's association inequality and the remainder by hand.

The inequality must be carried from the strong-coupling end of the sequence, where it is proved, into the scaling window of weak bare coupling, where asymptotic freedom ties the bare coupling to the spacing. Step 11 — Dobrushin's coefficient bounds the gap, and the chain lemma splits it into rung quantities
DATE: 1941 (Gelfand), 1956 (Dobrushin); the chain lemma 2026-10-28. STATUS: PROVED; the lemma's reading on a decimation is a MEASUREMENT.
The mathematics

Proposition (Dobrushin's coefficient bounds the gap). Let T be a transfer operator with a continuous, strictly positive kernel on a compact space X, with largest eigenvalue λ₀ and positive eigenfunction ψ₀, and let P(x, dy) = T(x, dy) ψ₀(y)/(λ₀ ψ₀(x)) be its Doob transform, a Markov kernel. For k ≥ 1 let δ(P^k) = sup_{x,y} ‖P^k(x, ·) − P^k(y, ·)‖_TV be Dobrushin's coefficient. Then every real eigenvalue λ ≠ λ₀ of T satisfies |λ|/λ₀ ≤ δ(P^k)^{1/k}, and when T is positive,
m_lat ≥ (1/k) log(1/δ(P^k)) for every k ≥ 1.

When X is finite, m_lat equals the limit of the right side as k → ∞. Proof. The Doob transform has the eigenvalues λ/λ₀ of T, with eigenfunctions u = ψ/ψ₀, which are bounded because ψ₀ is bounded below on the compact space. For a real bounded function u, P^k u(x) − P^k u(y) is the integral of u against the signed measure P^k(x, ·) − P^k(y, ·), of total mass zero and total variation at most 2δ(P^k), so osc(P^k u) ≤ δ(P^k) osc(u). If Pu = μu with μ real and u nonconstant, then osc(P^k u) = |μ|^k osc(u), whence |μ|^k ≤ δ(P^k). When T is positive every eigenvalue is non-negative, and the bound at λ₁ is the display. When X is finite, δ(P^k) is the norm of P^k on the signed measures of total mass zero, on which the spectrum of P is that of T/λ₀ with the simple eigenvalue 1 removed, and Gelfand's spectral-radius formula gives the limit. ∎ (R. L. Dobrushin, "Central limit theorem for nonstationary Markov chains. I, II", Theory Probab. Appl. 1 (1956), 65–80 and 329–383; I. Gelfand, "Normierte Ringe", Mat. Sbornik 9 (51) (1941), 3–24.) A certified bound δ(P^k) ≤ e^{−k m a_j} for the Doob chain of every rung's transfer matrix therefore gives the gap m_lat(j) ≥ m a_j of Step 10.

A single coefficient δ(P^k) is a global quantity, and on a lattice of many sites it is close to one at every accessible k. The renormalisation group splits it into rung quantities that can each be certified.

Proposition (the chain lemma). Let X be a finite state space, P the Doob chain of a transfer matrix on X with stationary law π, and b : X → Y a block map with fibres F_y = b^{−1}(y) and conditional laws π(· | y). Let (b_*μ)(y′) = μ(F_{y′}), and define the lumped chain P′(y, ·) = Σ_{x∈b⁻¹(y)} π(x | y)(b_*P²)(x, ·), so that one coarse step is two fine steps; for k ≥ 1 put Q = P′^k. With ‖μ − ν‖_TV = ½ Σ|μ − ν|, define the fibre forgetting η_k, the largest of ‖P^{2k}(x, ·) − P^{2k}(x′, ·)‖_TV over pairs x, x′ in one fibre; the lumping defect ε_k, the largest of ‖(b_*P^{2k})(x, ·) − Q(b(x), ·)‖_TV over x; and the fibre equilibration θ_k, the largest of ‖P^{2k}(x, · | y′) − π(· | y′)‖_TV over x and the fibres y′ that P^{2k}(x, ·) charges, where P^{2k}(x, · | y′) is P^{2k}(x, ·) conditioned on F_{y′}. Let M_k be the 2 × 2 matrix with rows (δ(Q) + 2ε_k, 2θ_k) and (η_k, 2η_k). Then
where ρ(M_k) = ½[(d + 2η_k) + √((d − 2η_k)² + 8θ_k η_k)] is the spectral radius of M_k and d = δ(Q) + 2ε_k.

Proof. For g : X → ℝ let ḡ(y) = Σ_{x∈b⁻¹(y)} π(x | y) g(x), a = osc(ḡ), s = max_y osc(g restricted to F_y) and r = g − ḡ∘b, so that |r| ≤ s and r has mean zero under every π(· | y). First, P^{2k}(ḡ∘b)(x) = Σ_{y′}(b_*P^{2k})(x, y′) ḡ(y′) = (Qḡ)(b(x)) + e₁(x), where e₁(x) integrates ḡ against a signed measure of total mass zero and total variation at most ε_k, so |e₁| ≤ ε_k a. Second, P^{2k} r(x) = Σ_{y′}(b_*P^{2k})(x, y′) Σ_{x′∈b⁻¹(y′)} P^{2k}(x, x′ | y′) r(x′), and because r has mean zero under π(· | y′) the inner sum equals Σ_{x′}[P^{2k}(x, x′ | y′) − π(x′ | y′)] r(x′), of modulus at most θ_k s; so e₂ = P^{2k} r satisfies |e₂| ≤ θ_k s. Hence P^{2k} g = (Qḡ)∘b + e₁ + e₂. For g′ = P^{2k} g write a′ and s′ for its two oscillations. The fibre mean of g′ is Qḡ plus a function bounded by ε_k a + θ_k s, and osc(Qḡ) ≤ δ(Q) osc(ḡ), so a′ ≤ (δ(Q) + 2ε_k) a + 2θ_k s. For x, x′ in one fibre, |g′(x) − g′(x′)| ≤ η_k osc(g) ≤ η_k(a + 2s), so s′ ≤ η_k(a + 2s). Finally osc(g′) ≤ a′ + 2s′. Since δ(P^{2k}) is the supremum of osc(P^{2k} g) over osc(g) ≤ 1, and osc(g) ≤ 1 gives a, s ≤ 1, the first inequality follows. The entries of M_k are non-negative, so the componentwise bounds (a′, s′) ≤ M_k(a, s) chain: applying P^{2k} j times with the same k at every step, against the same Q, so that the rung quantities are fixed, gives osc(P^{2kj} g) ≤ (1, 2) M_k^j (1, 1)^T for osc(g) ≤ 1. The first proposition applied to P^{2kj} then gives (λ₁/λ₀)^{2kj} ≤ δ(P^{2kj}) ≤ (1, 2) M_k^j (1, 1)^T ≤ C · j · ρ(M_k)^j, the factor j present only where M_k is not diagonalisable, and the j-th root removes it: this is the second inequality, of which the third is the logarithm. ∎

The lemma's scope. The lumping defect accumulates over the coarse chain's mixing time, since ε_k ≤ k ε₁ by telescoping and ε₁ ≤ η₁, so on a chain of n levels down to the mixing scale the level m must certify ε_m 2^{n−m} < 1. The instrument is therefore finite: it reaches a gap through finitely many certified levels, and the continuum end of the sequence lies beyond it, with the renormalised trajectory of Step 10. Its place in Step 9 is exact: the inequality m_lat(j) ≥ m a_j at rung j holds as soon as one k and one block map certify ρ(M_k) ≤ e^{−2k m a_j} there. Read in double precision on the decimation of the Z₂ transfer matrix of the 2 × 4 cross-section to 2 × 2, the lemma gives m_lat ≥ 1.538 at u = ⅓ against the certified gap 3.831, and m_lat ≥ 0.867 at u = ½ against the certified gap 1.763, u = e^{−2β}.
The explanation

The first proposition turns the gap into mixing: the Doob transform makes the transfer matrix a Markov chain with the vacuum as its stationary law, and the oscillation of a function contracts under one step by Dobrushin's coefficient, which the eigenfunctions of the chain cannot escape. The second is the renormalisation group read on that chain: a coarse chain on the block variables, one coarse step being two fine steps, plus three defects — what a fibre forgets of its starting point (η), how far the lumped chain is from a Markov chain on the blocks (ε), and how fast a fibre equilibrates (θ) — and the whole contraction is the spectral radius of a 2 × 2 matrix of those four numbers. The reading on the Z₂ decimation shows the lemma's two faces at once: it certifies a positive gap from rung quantities, and it certifies less than the exact gap, by a factor near two, because the coarse chain's own coefficient is read with the defects added rather than resolved.

Let m_n(G′) be the moments of χ under the uniform measure on G′ and t the largest integer with m_k(G′) = m_k(SU(2)) for every k ≤ t. Then t is odd, and the functions Δ_tube(b) = −4 log(c_χ/c₀) of G′ and of SU(2) satisfy

The integer t is the design strength of G′ as a set of points of the three-sphere SU(2). Proof. Since −1 ∈ G′ and χ(−g) = −χ(g), the odd moments vanish, so t is odd and every series below is even. Let Z(b) = Σ_n m_n b^n/n! be the normalised partition function. Then c_χ/c₀ = ½(log Z)′(b), and since m₂ = 1, c_χ/c₀ = (b/2)(1 + u(b)) with u(b) = O(b²). The moments of G′ and of SU(2) agree through order t, so log Z^{G′} − log Z^{SU(2)} = δ b^{t+1}/(t+1)! + O(b^{t+3}). Since u = (log Z)′/b − 1, differentiating and dividing by b gives u^{G′} − u^{SU(2)} = δ b^{t−1}/t! + O(b^{t+1}), and since Δ_tube = −4 log(b/2) − 4 log(1 + u) with u = O(b²), the display follows. The moment m_n(G′) is the multiplicity of the trivial representation of G′ in the n-th tensor power of the fundamental representation. By the Clebsch–Gordan rule the moments agree through order n exactly when no irreducible representation of SU(2) of spin j with 1 ≤ 2j ≤ n has a nonzero G′-invariant vector. The harmonic polynomials of degree 2j on the three-sphere are the matrix coefficients of spin j, and their average over G′ is the projection onto the G′-invariant vectors, so the same condition says that G′ is a design of strength n. ∎ The moments of SU(2) are the Catalan numbers 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132 at n = 2, 4, …, 12; those of the quaternion group Q₈ and of the binary tetrahedral, octahedral and icosahedral groups 2T, 2O, 2I are 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024; 1, 2, 6, 22, 86, 342; 1, 2, 5, 15, 51, 187; and 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 133. Hence, exactly: Q₈ (order 8) has t = 3, m₄ = 4 against 2, δ = 2, first defect −4/3; 2T (order 24) has t = 5, m₆ = 6 against 5, δ = 1, first defect −1/30; 2O (order 48) has t = 7, m₈ = 15 against 14, δ = 1, first defect −1/1260; 2I (order 120) has t = 11, m₁₂ = 133 against 132, δ = 1, first defect −1/9979200. The finite groups therefore approximate the strong-coupling gap of SU(2) to an order fixed by their design strength, with an exactly known first defect.

The gap by counting. J. Sylvester, Philosophical Magazine 4 (1852), 138–142), so that every gap is certified to thirteen or fourteen decimal places by counting alone, with no limit taken. At all fourteen cells the brackets contain the eigenvalues computed to forty-five digits by a second engine that shares no computation with the first, and they meet a third, independently certified set of intervals. On the 3 × 3 cross-section at e^{−2β} = ½ the gap is 4.391458312669 in lattice units.

Phys. 12 (1971), 2259–2272) the gap of the Z₂ gauge theory in 2 + 1 dimensions at coupling β is the inverse correlation length of the three-dimensional Ising model at the dual coupling K*, with tanh K* = e^{−2β}. Arisue and K. Tabata, Nucl. Phys. B435 (1995), 555–566), and, solving that published relation for the coefficients that no cross-section of side at most four can read, the expansion on the infinite lattice is

For the SU(2) Wilson theory in 2 + 1 dimensions on the spatial torus of side two, in the temporal gauge, with the transfer matrix written in the spin-network basis truncated at spin j ≤ 1, a space of 2,018 states, and at j ≤ 3/2, a space of 33,342 states, the spectrum is read within the truncation and two facts are proved about the operator. The explanation

These are the instruments with which the strong-coupling end is read exactly, and each is stated at the strength of its proof or of its record. The shadow ladder is a theorem: a finite subgroup of SU(2) is a spherical design of odd strength t, and its strong-coupling gap on a tube agrees with SU(2)'s to order b^{t−1} with a first defect that is a ratio of two integers — the binary icosahedral group, a design of strength 11, parts from SU(2) only at b¹⁰ and by one part in 9,979,200. The gap by counting is a certificate: Sylvester's law of inertia turns a lattice gap into a count of signs of an integer matrix, so that no rounding and no limit enters the thirteen certified places; and the duality expansion is the same gap read against a published series it has no computation in common with, ten coefficients meeting. The tube is a reading, not a theorem, and it is carried at both of its cutoffs with the cutoff named, because the truncation moves the numbers by six per cent and more; what it proves is structural — the lumping by the centre flux is exact — and what it reads is the first non-abelian instance of the rate the chain lemma must carry. The machine-checked theorems are the finite forms of the arguments of this document, each in the kernel with no axiom and no unproved step.

The mathematics

Proposition (the tilt lemmas). Let p and p′ be probability measures on a compact space X, ρ a bounded measurable function on X with oscillation osc ρ = sup ρ − inf ρ, and T_ρ p = e^ρ p/p(e^ρ) the tilt of p by ρ. Then
‖T_ρ p − p‖_TV ≤ 1 − e^{−osc ρ}, ‖T_ρ p − T_ρ p′‖_TV ≤ e^{osc ρ} ‖p − p′‖_TV.

Consequently, let W be a positive weight on the configurations of finitely many sites with compact spin spaces, with interdependence matrix C, and δ a bounded function of the configuration; let o_y(δ) be the supremum, over configurations, of the oscillation of δ in the variable at y, and Δ_{yy′}(δ) the supremum, over pairs of configurations differing only at y′, of the oscillation in the variable at y of the difference of the two restrictions of δ. Then the weight W e^δ has interdependence matrix at most e^{o_y(δ)} C(y, y′) + 1 − e^{−Δ_{yy′}(δ)}. Proof. Normalise ρ so that its infimum is 0 and its supremum is o = osc ρ; the tilt is unchanged. Then e^ρ takes values in [1, e^o] and A = p(e^ρ) lies in the same interval, so T_ρ p has density e^ρ/A ≥ e^{−o} with respect to p; for every measurable set B, p(B) − (T_ρ p)(B) ≤ (1 − e^{−o}) p(B) ≤ 1 − e^{−o}, and the supremum over B is the first inequality. For the second, let p_u = p + u(p′ − p) for 0 ≤ u ≤ 1 and q_u = T_ρ p_u, with A_u = p_u(e^ρ) ≥ 1. For a measurable set B, q_u(B) = p_u(e^ρ 1_B)/A_u, and differentiating in u, (d/du) q_u(B) = (1/A_u) ∫ (1_B − q_u(B)) e^ρ d(p′ − p). The integrand (1_B − q_u(B)) e^ρ takes values in [1 − q_u(B), (1 − q_u(B)) e^o] on B and in [−q_u(B) e^o, −q_u(B)] off B, so its oscillation is at most e^o; and the integral of a function of oscillation at most c against a signed measure of total mass zero is at most c times half the total variation of that measure, that is, c‖p′ − p‖_TV. Hence |dq_u(B)/du| ≤ e^o‖p′ − p‖_TV, and integrating from 0 to 1 gives |(T_ρ p′)(B) − (T_ρ p)(B)| ≤ e^o‖p′ − p‖_TV for every B, which is the second inequality. For the last assertion, fix a site y and a configuration ω of the other sites, and let p_ω be the conditional law of the variable at y under W; the conditional law under W e^δ is T_ρ p_ω with ρ the restriction of δ to the variable at y at ω, of oscillation at most o_y(δ). If ω′ differs from ω only at y′, with restriction ρ′, then T_{ρ′} p_{ω′} = T_{ρ′−ρ}(T_ρ p_{ω′}), so by the triangle inequality and the two inequalities just proved, ‖T_ρ p_ω − T_{ρ′} p_{ω′}‖_TV ≤ e^o‖p_ω − p_{ω′}‖_TV + 1 − e^{−osc(ρ′−ρ)} ≤ e^o C(y, y′) + 1 − e^{−Δ}, with o = o_y(δ) and Δ = Δ_{yy′}(δ). ∎

Hypothesis I (the blocked bound). There are numbers κ > 0 and α < 1 and a rung j₀ such that at every rung j ≥ j₀, on every lattice of the construction, Σ_{y′} C^λ_j(y, y′) e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ α for every coarse point y.

Hypothesis II (the fibre clustering). There are a number ρ′ < 1, a constant K′ and a rung j₀ such that at every rung j ≥ j₀, on every lattice of the construction, for every coarse configuration v and all bounded observables f and g, with d the distance between S(f) and S(g): (a) |ν_j(fg | v) − ν_j(f | v) ν_j(g | v)| ≤ K′ N(f) ‖f‖ ‖g‖ ρ′^d; (b) the fibre mean F(v) = ν_j(f | v), as a function of the coarse configuration, satisfies δ_y(F) ≤ K′ N(f) ‖f‖ ρ′^r for every coarse point y, where r is the distance from y to S(f).

Hypothesis I is the second link of Step 10 in its finite form: a statement about the conditional law of one coarse variable at one fixed physical scale, with the exponential weight that fixes the range, and with constants independent of the cutoff and of the volume. Hypothesis II is the ultraviolet half of the chain at the scales below a_c: with the coarse variables held fixed, the field inside the blocks clusters at the block scale, and its means depend on distant coarse variables only through an exponentially small tail. It is demanded for every coarse configuration, the adversarial ones included, because a single-site criterion conditions on the worst case; this is where it exceeds the small-field expansions, which control the fluctuation field in typical backgrounds and the large fields by their probability, and it is named here as the demand it is. It cannot be weakened to typical coarse configurations with the frustrated ones priced by their probability: the Ising model at low temperature on the tori (ℤ/Lℤ)^d, d ≥ 2, satisfies every such form with both prices as small as one likes, and has long-range order. On the event that the 2(2d − 1) outer neighbours of an adjacent pair carry one sign, the maximal correlation of the pair given the rest is sinh 2β/(cosh 2(2d − 1)β + cosh 2β) ≤ e^{−4(d−1)β}, every function of a two-valued variable being affine; the complementary event lies in the union of the 4d − 1 events that one bond of the pair's star is unsatisfied, and by the chessboard estimate its probability is at most (4d − 1) · 2^{1/L} e^{−2β}, with chessboard weight at most 2^{3^d} e^{−2β/c_d} for a constant c_d depending on d alone; Peierls' argument gives σ₀σ_x mean at least ½ for every x and L once β is large (R. Peierls, Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 32 (1936), 477–481; R. B. Griffiths, Phys. Rev. 136 (1964), A437–A439; J. Fröhlich, R. Israel, E. H. Lieb and B. Simon, Comm. Math. Phys. 62 (1978), 1–34). More generally, no condition that depends on a measure only through the joint law of its single-pair conditional coefficients implies decay of correlations: in infinite volume μ⁺ and ½(μ⁺ + μ⁻) are Gibbs measures of one specification and give that law the same distribution, a maximal correlation being invariant under a bijection of each variable's values, while only the first has decaying truncated correlations. The supremum in the interdependence matrix runs over exactly the configurations that Dobrushin's comparison visits when it telescopes between two environments typical of different phases, every intermediate one frustrated. Neither hypothesis refers to a limit. Their consequence is the gap.

Hypothesis I read on the effective action. Write the blocked measure as λ_j(dv) = e^{−A} dv with respect to the product over the blocks of a fixed reference measure on V, so that A = A_j(v) is the effective action at the coarse scale, and let Δ_{yy′}(A) be its mixed second difference in the sense of the tilt lemmas: the supremum, over coarse configurations differing only at y′, of the oscillation in v_y of the difference of the two actions. The conditional law of v_y under one of the two configurations is the tilt of its conditional law under the other by that difference, so the first inequality of the tilt lemmas gives C^λ_j(y, y′) ≤ 1 − e^{−Δ} with Δ = Δ_{yy′}(A). Hypothesis I is therefore a bound on the mixed second differences of the effective action between blocks, weighted by their distance: the influence functional of Step 10's second link, and the number that a certificate of that link must deliver at the coarse scale. The hypothesis cannot be stated on the fine measure with the whole configuration of a block as a site's variable: that form's interdependence coefficient between adjacent blocks is the total variation between two laws of all the links of a block under outside data differing on a whole neighbouring face, and as the spacing tends to zero that face carries ever more links, the two laws become distinguishable almost surely by an average over the face, and the coefficient tends to one at every coupling. Whole-block total variation is the one norm that does not survive large blocks, and the hypothesis is therefore stated on the coarse variables, whose type is fixed, with the field inside the blocks entering through its clustering alone.
The explanation

The theorem places the four-dimensional gap at one remove from a finite statement. Hypotheses I and II concern the conditional law of one coarse variable and the field inside one block, at a fixed physical scale, with constants uniform in the cutoff, and nothing in them refers to a limit; their consequence is the unique vacuum, the cluster property and the mass gap of every limit point, with the gap's value m = (1/a_c) min(κ, log(1/ρ′)). The mechanism is Dobrushin's comparison: the blocked measure is a finite system of compact variables, a tilt of it by the fibre mean of g changes each conditional law by a total variation that Hypothesis II(b) makes exponentially small away from g's support, and Hypothesis I makes the comparison's series D = Σ(C^λ)^n converge with exponential decay. The two hypotheses are the whole of what remains, and the paragraph on the Ising model fixes why they are stated at the supremum and not at typical configurations: a weakening to typical configurations is satisfied by a model with long-range order.
