Step 14 — The reduction in L²: the gap is a norm, the conditional maximal correlation matrix, and the fibre clause averaged over the blocked measure
DATE: 1941 (Gebelein), 1959 (Rényi), 1969 (Halmos), 2011 (Kassabov); the reduction in L² 2026-10-28. STATUS: PROVED — an implication with its two hypotheses named.
The mathematics

Proposition (the gap is an L² norm). Let T be a transfer operator on a compact space X with kernel T(x, dy) = t(x, y) dy, t continuous, strictly positive and symmetric, and T positive as an operator on L²(dy); let λ₀ > λ₁ be its two largest eigenvalues, ψ₀ the positive eigenfunction normalised in L²(dy), π(dx) = ψ₀(x)² dx, and P the Doob transform of Step 11. Then P is self-adjoint on L²(π); on L²₀(π), the functions of π-mean zero, ‖P^k‖ = (λ₁/λ₀)^k for every k ≥ 1, so that m_lat = −log ‖P‖_{L²₀(π)}; ‖P^k‖_{L²₀(π)} ≤ δ(P^k); and, with the eigenvalues λ_i of T counted with multiplicity, ∫ χ²(P^k(x, ·) ‖ π) π(dx) = Tr T^{2k}/λ₀^{2k} − 1 = Σ_{i≥1} (λ_i/λ₀)^{2k}. Proof. For bounded u and w, ∫ w · Pu dπ = λ₀⁻¹ ∬ w(x)ψ₀(x) t(x, y) ψ₀(y)u(y) dx dy, which is symmetric in u and w; so P is self-adjoint on L²(π). Multiplication by ψ₀ is a unitary map U of L²(π) onto L²(dx), ψ₀ being continuous and bounded below on the compact space X, and (T/λ₀)(ψ₀u) = ψ₀ Pu, that is UPU⁻¹ = T/λ₀. The map U carries the constants to ψ₀ and L²₀(π) onto the orthogonal complement of ψ₀, so P on L²₀(π) is unitarily equivalent to T/λ₀ on that complement, a compact positive operator whose norm is its largest eigenvalue λ₁/λ₀; powers pass through the equivalence. For an eigenvalue λ ≠ 0 of T with eigenfunction ψ, the eigenfunction ψ/ψ₀ of P is continuous, hence bounded, and it is nonconstant when λ ≠ λ₀, so the oscillation argument of Step 11 gives |λ/λ₀|^k ≤ δ(P^k) for every eigenvalue λ ≠ λ₀ of T; the norm of the self-adjoint P^k on L²₀(π) is the largest of these numbers. Finally P^k(x, dy) has density p_k(x, y) = t_k(x, y)/(λ₀^k ψ₀(x)ψ₀(y)) with respect to π, t_k the kernel of T^k, so ∬ p_k² dπ dπ = λ₀^{−2k} ∬ t_k(x, y)² dx dy = λ₀^{−2k} Tr T^{2k} = Σ_i (λ_i/λ₀)^{2k}, the operator T^k being Hilbert–Schmidt with continuous symmetric kernel; since ∫ p_k(x, y) π(dy) = 1 for every x, ∬ (p_k − 1)² dπ dπ = Tr T^{2k}/λ₀^{2k} − 1, and the inner integral is χ²(P^k(x, ·) ‖ π). ∎ The average is at least the multiplicity of λ₁ times (λ₁/λ₀)^{2k}, so it controls the gap only once the decay beats that multiplicity; the norm carries no multiplicity, and Step 11's proposition dominates it by a supremum over pairs of starting points.

The currency. For the reduction in L² the blocked measure is assumed to have the form (S): λ_j(dv) = e^{−A_j(v)} Π_{y∈Y} m(dv_y), with m a Borel probability measure on V, Y the set of coarse points of the lattice, and A_j a measurable function finite Πm-almost everywhere, the effective action at the coarse scale. A block map is translation covariant when it commutes with the translations of the lattice by multiples of a_c; its blocked measure is then invariant under the translations of Y. For a rung j and a lattice of the construction, the inner product of L²(λ_j) is ⟨F, G⟩ = λ_j(F̄G). For y ∈ Y let H_y be the closed subspace of L²(λ_j) of functions of v_{yᶜ} = (v_z)_{z≠y}, K_y the orthogonal projection onto it, which is the conditional expectation K_y F = λ_j(F | v_{yᶜ}), and Q_y = I − K_y. The L² local fluctuation of F ∈ L²(λ_j) at y is ℓ_y(F) = ‖Q_y F‖ = λ_j(Var_{λ_j}(F | v_{yᶜ}))^{1/2}; it vanishes unless F depends on v_y, it equals ℓ_y(F̄), and for bounded F it is at most δ_y(F)/2 when F is real and at most δ_y(F)/√2 in general. For distinct y, y′ write ξ = (v_z)_{z≠y,y′} for the coarse environment of the pair, π_ξ for a version of the conditional law of (v_y, v_{y′}) given ξ, and ρ_ξ(y, y′) = sup{|Cov_{π_ξ}(f(v_y), g(v_{y′}))| : Var_{π_ξ} f = Var_{π_ξ} g = 1} for its maximal correlation (H. Gebelein, Z. Angew. Math. Mech. 21 (1941), 364–379; A. Rényi, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 10 (1959), 441–451), zero when v_y or v_{y′} is almost surely constant under π_ξ, a countable supremum over f and g in a uniformly dense subset of the continuous functions on V, hence measurable in ξ. The conditional maximal correlation matrix of the blocked measure is
R_j(y, y′) = ess sup_ξ ρ_ξ(y, y′), R_j(y, y) = 0,
the essential supremum taken under λ_j; it is symmetric, its entries lie in [0, 1], and it does not depend on the versions.

Hypothesis I′ (the blocked bound in L²). There are numbers κ > 0 and α < 1 and a rung j₀ such that at every rung j ≥ j₀, on every lattice of the construction, Σ_{y′} R_j(y, y′) e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ α for every coarse point y. Hypothesis II′ (the fibre clustering, averaged over the blocked measure). There are a number ρ′ < 1, a constant K′ and a rung j₀ such that at every rung j ≥ j₀, on every lattice of the construction, for all bounded observables f and g, with d the distance between S(f) and S(g): (a) |λ_j(ν_j(fg | ·) − ν_j(f | ·) ν_j(g | ·))| ≤ K′ N(f) ‖f‖ ‖g‖ ρ′^d; (b) the fibre mean F = ν_j(f | ·), as a function of the coarse configuration, satisfies ℓ_y(F) ≤ K′ N(f) ‖f‖ ρ′^r for every coarse point y, where r is the distance from y to S(f). Both hypotheses involve the fibre measure and the conditional laws of λ_j only through λ_j-integrals and λ_j-essential suprema, so they do not depend on the versions; the one supremum in them is the essential supremum over the coarse environment, and in Hypothesis II′ an adversarial coarse configuration enters weighted by its probability. Hypothesis II implies Hypothesis II′ with the same ρ′ and K′, since the λ_j-mean of a function is at most its supremum and ℓ_y(F) ≤ δ_y(F)/√2 ≤ δ_y(F). Hypothesis I implies Hypothesis I′ with the same κ and α when the block map is translation covariant, by the currency inequality below.

Lemma (two projections). Let P and Q be orthogonal projections on a Hilbert space, N = ran P ∩ ran Q, P_N the orthogonal projection onto N, and c = ‖PQ − P_N‖, the cosine of the Friedrichs angle between ran P and ran Q. Then for every vector F, ‖(I − Q)PF‖ ≤ ‖(I − Q)F‖ + c ‖(I − P)F‖. Proof. By Halmos' theorem on two subspaces (P. R. Halmos, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 144 (1969), 381–389; K. Friedrichs, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 41 (1937), 321–364) the space is the orthogonal sum of ran P ∩ ran Q, ran P ∩ ker Q, ker P ∩ ran Q, ker P ∩ ker Q and a generic part unitarily equivalent to K ⊕ K, on which P acts as the matrix with rows (I, 0), (0, 0) and Q as the matrix with rows (C², CS), (CS, S²), with C = cos Θ and S = sin Θ for a positive operator Θ on K with 0 < Θ < π/2 and trivial kernels of Θ and π/2 − Θ; every summand reduces P and Q. On the four trivial summands PQ − P_N vanishes, and on the generic part P_N = 0 and the norm of PQ is that of the row (C², CS), which is ‖C‖; so c = ‖C‖ when the generic part is not zero. On ran P ∩ ran Q, (I − Q)PF = 0; on ran P ∩ ker Q, (I − Q)PF = F = (I − Q)F; on the two summands inside ker P, PF = 0: on each the inequality holds with 0 in place of c. On the generic part write F = (x, y). Then I − Q is the matrix with rows (S², −CS), (−CS, C²), so (I − Q)PF = (S·Sx, −C·Sx), of norm ‖Sx‖ since C² + S² = I, and (I − Q)F = (S(Sx − Cy), −C(Sx − Cy)), of norm ‖Sx − Cy‖. Hence ‖(I − Q)PF‖ = ‖Sx‖ ≤ ‖Sx − Cy‖ + ‖Cy‖ ≤ ‖(I − Q)F‖ + c‖y‖, and ‖y‖ = ‖(I − P)F‖. The summands are orthogonal and preserved by P and Q, so Minkowski's inequality over them gives the claim. ∎

Lemma (the angle between two coarse variables). For distinct y, y′ the cosine c(y, y′) of the Friedrichs angle between H_y and H_{y′} is at most R_j(y, y′). Consequently, for every F ∈ L²(λ_j), ℓ_y(K_y F) = 0 and ℓ_{y′}(K_y F) ≤ ℓ_{y′}(F) + R_j(y, y′) ℓ_y(F). Proof. The intersection H_y ∩ H_{y′} contains every function of ξ. The cosine c(y, y′) is the supremum of |⟨F, G⟩| over unit vectors F ∈ H_y orthogonal to H_y ∩ H_{y′} and G ∈ H_{y′} orthogonal to H_y ∩ H_{y′}. Such an F is a function of (v_{y′}, ξ) orthogonal to every function of ξ, so λ_j(F | ξ) = 0: for λ_j-almost every ξ, F(·, ξ) has mean zero under the law of v_{y′} under π_ξ. Likewise G is a function of (v_y, ξ) with G(·, ξ) of mean zero under the law of v_y under π_ξ. Disintegrating λ_j over ξ, ⟨F, G⟩ = ∫ λ_j(dξ) ∫ π_ξ(dv_y dv_{y′}) F̄(v_{y′}, ξ) G(v_y, ξ), and the inner integral is at most ρ_ξ(y, y′) times the product of the norms of F(·, ξ) and G(·, ξ) in L²(π_ξ), by the definition of the maximal correlation. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality over ξ gives |⟨F, G⟩| ≤ R_j(y, y′)‖F‖‖G‖, which is the first assertion. The second is ‖Q_y K_y F‖ = 0, and the third is the two-projections lemma with P = K_y and Q = K_{y′}. ∎

Proposition (the fluctuation vector decays). Let ℒ = Σ_{y∈Y} (K_y − I), a bounded self-adjoint operator on L²(λ_j), and P_t = e^{tℒ} the semigroup of the heat-bath dynamics that resamples each coarse variable from its conditional law at rate one. Write ℓ(F) = (ℓ_y(F))_{y∈Y}. Then for every F ∈ L²(λ_j) and every t ≥ 0, componentwise, ℓ(P_t F) ≤ e^{−t(I − R_j)} ℓ(F). Proof. For 0 < h ≤ 1/|Y|, I + hℒ = (1 − |Y|h)I + h Σ_y K_y with non-negative coefficients. Since ℓ_z is a seminorm, ℓ_z(K_z G) = 0, and ℓ_z(K_y G) ≤ ℓ_z(G) + R_j(y, z)ℓ_y(G) for y ≠ z by the angle lemma, ℓ_z((I + hℒ)G) ≤ (1 − |Y|h)ℓ_z(G) + h(|Y| − 1)ℓ_z(G) + h Σ_{y≠z} R_j(y, z)ℓ_y(G) = (((1 − h)I + hR_j)ℓ(G))_z, the matrix R_j being symmetric. The matrix (1 − h)I + hR_j has non-negative entries, so it preserves the componentwise order, and induction gives ℓ((I + tℒ/n)^n F) ≤ ((1 − t/n)I + (t/n)R_j)^n ℓ(F) for n ≥ t|Y|. As n → ∞, (I + tℒ/n)^n → e^{tℒ} in operator norm, ℒ being bounded, each ℓ_z is continuous on L²(λ_j), and ((1 − t/n)I + (t/n)R_j)^n → e^{−t(I−R_j)}. ∎
Theorem (the covariance theorem in L²). Suppose that ∩_{y∈Y} H_y consists of the constants and that the spectral radius ρ(R_j) of R_j is less than one. Then for all F and G in L²(λ_j),
|λ_j(FG) − λ_j(F)λ_j(G)| ≤ Σ_{x,y∈Y} ℓ_x(F) D(x, y) ℓ_y(G), D = (I − R_j)^{−1} = Σ_{n≥0} R_j^n,

with D entrywise non-negative, and Var_{λ_j}(F) ≤ (1 − ρ(R_j))^{−1} Σ_{y∈Y} λ_j(Var_{λ_j}(F | v_{yᶜ})). If moreover Σ_{y′} R_j(y, y′) e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ α < 1 for every y, then ρ(R_j) ≤ α and D(x, y) ≤ e^{−κ|x−y|}/(1 − α). Under (S) the intersection ∩_y H_y consists of the constants. Proof. The Dirichlet form of the dynamics is E(F, G) = ⟨F, −ℒG⟩ = Σ_y ⟨Q_y F, Q_y G⟩, so |E(F, G)| ≤ Σ_y ℓ_y(F)ℓ_y(G). The kernel of ℒ is ∩_y H_y, since ℒF = 0 gives Σ_y ‖Q_y F‖² = ⟨F, −ℒF⟩ = 0; it consists of the constants by assumption, so the spectral theorem for the bounded self-adjoint operator ℒ ≤ 0 gives P_t G → λ_j(G) in L²(λ_j) as t → ∞. Since λ_j(FG) = ⟨F̄, G⟩ and (d/dt)⟨F̄, P_t G⟩ = −E(F̄, P_t G), λ_j(FG) − λ_j(F)λ_j(G) = ∫₀^∞ E(F̄, P_t G) dt, and by the decay proposition, with ℓ_y(F̄) = ℓ_y(F), |E(F̄, P_t G)| ≤ Σ_y ℓ_y(F)(e^{−t(I−R_j)}ℓ(G))_y. The matrix R_j is symmetric with non-negative entries and spectral radius less than one, so e^{−t(I−R_j)} = e^{−t}e^{tR_j} has non-negative entries and ∫₀^∞ e^{−t(I−R_j)} dt = (I − R_j)⁻¹ = Σ_n R_j^n; this is the first display. For the variance, (d/dt)‖P_t F − λ_j(F)‖² = −2E(P_t F, P_t F) = −2|ℓ(P_t F)|², with |·| the euclidean norm on ℝ^Y; the componentwise domination by a non-negative vector gives |ℓ(P_t F)| ≤ |e^{−t(I−R_j)}ℓ(F)| ≤ e^{−t(1−ρ(R_j))}|ℓ(F)|, the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric non-negative R_j being its spectral radius, and integration over [0, ∞) gives Var(F) ≤ (1 − ρ(R_j))⁻¹|ℓ(F)|², the second inequality. Under the weighted row-sum bound put R̃(y, y′) = R_j(y, y′)e^{κ|y−y′|}, with row sums at most α; since |y − y″| ≤ |y − y′| + |y′ − y″|, induction on n gives R_j^n(y, y′)e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ R̃^n(y, y′), and the row sums of R̃^n are at most α^n, so D(x, y)e^{κ|x−y|} ≤ Σ_n α^n = 1/(1 − α), while ρ(R_j) is at most the largest row sum of R_j, hence at most α. Under (S), λ_j and Πm have the same null sets; a function in ∩_y H_y agrees Πm-almost everywhere, for each y, with a function not depending on v_y, and integrating out the coordinates one at a time with Fubini's theorem on the product measure shows that it is Πm-almost everywhere constant. ∎ The variance inequality in its sharper quadratic form Var(F) ≤ ℓ(F)ᵀ(I − R_j)⁻¹ℓ(F) is M. Kassabov's theorem on arrangements of subspaces (Groups Geom. Dyn. 5 (2011), 445–477, Theorem 5.1), read for the arrangement of the H_y with Friedrichs' angles; the covariance bound in total variation, with Dobrushin's oscillations and interdependence matrix in place of the local fluctuations and R_j, is H. Föllmer's (J. Funct. Anal. 46 (1982), 387–395) and H. Künsch's (Comm. Math. Phys. 84 (1982), 207–222); the two-sided covariance bound above in L², with the exponential decay of (I − R_j)⁻¹ under the weighted row sums, does not follow from the quadratic form, which by polarisation loses the decay, and it is the form the reduction uses.

Proposition (the currency inequality). With versions of the conditional laws λ_j(dv_y | v) defined for every coarse configuration, as in Step 6, for distinct y and y′, R_j(y, y′)² ≤ C^λ_j(y, y′) C^λ_j(y′, y), so that R_j(y, y′) ≤ ½(C^λ_j(y, y′) + C^λ_j(y′, y)). For a translation-covariant block map, Hypothesis I therefore implies Hypothesis I′ with the same κ and α. When V has two points the inequality cannot be improved. Proof. Fix y ≠ y′ and an environment ξ, and write X = v_y, X′ = v_{y′}. For λ_j-almost every ξ the single-site laws at the configurations (X, X′, ξ) are conditional laws of π_ξ, and the operator Mg(b) = ∫ λ_j(dv_y | X′ = b, ξ) ∫ λ_j(dv_{y′} | X = v_y, ξ) g(v_{y′}), which goes from X′ to X and back, is a Markov kernel defined at every point, self-adjoint on L²(π′_ξ), π′_ξ the law of X′ under π_ξ, with norm ρ_ξ(y, y′)² on the functions of mean zero: it is T*T for the conditional expectation T from functions of X′ to functions of X, whose norm on the functions of mean zero is the maximal correlation. Its kernel is the composition of two kernels whose Dobrushin coefficients are C_ξ(y | y′) = sup_{b,b′} ‖λ_j(dv_y | X′ = b, ξ) − λ_j(dv_y | X′ = b′, ξ)‖_TV ≤ C^λ_j(y, y′) and C_ξ(y′ | y) ≤ C^λ_j(y′, y), and Dobrushin's coefficient is submultiplicative, so δ(M) ≤ C^λ_j(y, y′)C^λ_j(y′, y). It remains to show that the norm of M on the functions of mean zero is at most δ(M). For a bounded g of mean zero and n ≥ 1 the oscillation argument of Step 11 gives osc(M^n g) ≤ δ(M)^n osc(g), and M^n g has mean zero, so its L² norm is at most sup|M^n g| ≤ osc(M^n g). If the spectral projection E of the self-adjoint M, restricted to the functions of mean zero, onto {|λ| ≥ δ(M) + ε} were not zero for some ε > 0, there would be a bounded g of mean zero with Eg ≠ 0, the bounded functions being dense, and ‖M^n g‖ ≥ (δ(M) + ε)^n‖Eg‖ would contradict ‖M^n g‖ ≤ δ(M)^n osc(g) for large n. Hence ρ_ξ(y, y′)² ≤ C^λ_j(y, y′)C^λ_j(y′, y) for λ_j-almost every ξ, the first assertion, and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives the second. For a translation-covariant block map the blocked measure is invariant under the translations of Y, so the translates of the given versions at one coarse point y₀ are versions at every coarse point; read with them, C^λ_j(y, y′) is the given matrix's entry at (y₀, y₀ + y′ − y), its weighted row and column sums all equal the weighted row sum of the given matrix at y₀, at most α under Hypothesis I, and the inequality holds for these versions as for any, R_j not depending on them; then Σ_{y′} R_j(y, y′)e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ ½ Σ_{y′}(C^λ_j(y, y′) + C^λ_j(y′, y))e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ α. When V = {0, 1}, write p_{ab} for the probability of X = a, X′ = b under π_ξ, p_{a·} and p_{·b} for its marginals, and Δ = p₁₁p₀₀ − p₁₀p₀₁; every function of a two-point variable is affine in its indicator, so ρ_ξ = |Δ|/(p_{1·}p_{0·}p_{·1}p_{·0})^{1/2}, while C_ξ(y | y′) = |p₁₁/p_{·1} − p₁₀/p_{·0}| = |Δ|/(p_{·1}p_{·0}) and C_ξ(y′ | y) = |Δ|/(p_{1·}p_{0·}), whose product is ρ_ξ². ∎

Theorem (the reduction of the gap to the blocked bound, in L²). Let a construction be blocked at the coarse scale a_c as in Step 13, with a block map whose blocked measures have the form (S), and suppose Hypotheses I′ and II′. Put ρ = max(e^{−κ}, ρ′). Then for every ρ₁ with ρ < ρ₁ < 1 there is a constant K, depending on ρ, ρ₁, α, K′, N(f), N(g), ‖f‖ and ‖g‖ and on nothing else, such that at every rung j ≥ j₀, on every lattice of the construction, for all bounded observables f and g, |S_j(fg) − S_j(f) S_j(g)| ≤ K ρ₁^d, with d the distance between S(f) and S(g); and every limit point of the construction's Schwinger functions, on the sector generated by the observables that are bounded uniformly in j, has a unique vacuum and a Hamiltonian with no spectrum in (0, m), with m = (1/a_c) min(κ, log(1/ρ′)), the number of Step 13. Proof. Fix j ≥ j₀, a lattice, and bounded observables f and g; write F(v) = ν_j(f | v) and G(v) = ν_j(g | v) for their fibre means, bounded by ‖f‖ and ‖g‖. The covariance splits along the block map, by the law of total covariance: μ_j(fg) − μ_j(f)μ_j(g) = [λ_j(FG) − λ_j(F)λ_j(G)] + λ_j(ν_j(fg | ·) − FG). The second term is at most K′N(f)‖f‖‖g‖ρ′^d by Hypothesis II′(a). For the first, Hypothesis I′ gives ρ(R_j) ≤ α < 1 and D(i, k) ≤ e^{−κ|i−k|}/(1 − α), (S) identifies ∩_y H_y with the constants, and the covariance theorem gives |λ_j(FG) − λ_j(F)λ_j(G)| ≤ Σ_{i,k} ℓ_i(F)D(i, k)ℓ_k(G). By Hypothesis II′(b), ℓ_i(F) ≤ K′N(f)‖f‖ρ′^{r_i} and ℓ_k(G) ≤ K′N(g)‖g‖ρ′^{r′_k}, with r_i the distance from i to S(f) and r′_k that from k to S(g), so that |λ_j(FG) − λ_j(F)λ_j(G)| ≤ (K′²N(f)N(g)‖f‖‖g‖/(1 − α)) Σ_{i,k} ρ^{e(i,k)}, e(i, k) = r_i + |i − k| + r′_k, ρ = max(e^{−κ}, ρ′) bounding the base of each of the three factors. By the triangle inequality e(i, k) ≥ d, and the number of pairs (i, k) with e(i, k) ≤ n is at most N(f)N(g)(2n + 1)⁸; hence the last sum is at most N(f)N(g) Σ_{n≥d}(2n + 1)⁸ρ^n, which is ρ^d times a polynomial in d and is therefore at most K₁ρ₁^d for every ρ₁ ∈ (ρ, 1), with K₁ depending on ρ, ρ₁, N(f) and N(g). Adding the second term gives the covariance inequality, with K = K′²N(f)N(g)‖f‖‖g‖K₁/(1 − α) + K′N(f)‖f‖‖g‖. For the gap, let f be an observable, bounded uniformly in j, whose links lie in the time interval [0, w]. The links of θf̄ lie in [−w, 0] and those of τ_t f in [t, t + w]; the block boundaries in time are the multiples of a_c and a link belongs to the block of its midpoint, so S(θf̄) lies in blocks of time index at most 0, S(τ_t f) in blocks of time index at least ⌊t/a_c⌋, and the distance between them is at least ⌊t/a_c⌋ ≥ t/a_c − 1. For t ∈ D and all large j, t is an integer multiple of a_j; the measure μ_j is invariant under the reflection θ and under the translation τ_t, so μ_j(θf̄) is the complex conjugate of μ_j(f) and μ_j(τ_t f) = μ_j(f), and the covariance inequality gives S_j(θf̄ · τ_t f) − |S_j(f)|² ≤ (K/ρ₁)e^{−m₁t} with m₁ = log(1/ρ₁)/a_c, the constant independent of j and of the lattice because N(f) and ‖f‖ are. This is the hypothesis of Step 9's theorem with r_j = 0 at every t ∈ D, so that theorem leaves no spectrum in (0, m₁) for every ρ₁ ∈ (ρ, 1), hence none in (0, m), m = log(1/ρ)/a_c. ∎

Proposition (the tilt lemma in L²). Let π be the law of a pair (X, W) of random variables with values in compact metric spaces, δ a bounded measurable function of (x, w), and π′ = e^δ π/π(e^δ) the tilt of π by δ. Put o_X = sup_w osc_x δ(x, w), o_W = sup_x osc_w δ(x, w), and Δ = sup_{w,w′} osc_x(δ(x, w) − δ(x, w′)), the mixed second difference of δ in the sense of Step 13. Then the maximal correlations of the two laws satisfy ρ(π′) ≤ e^{(o_X + o_W)/2} ρ(π) + 1 − e^{−2Δ}. Proof. If (X, W) is almost surely constant under π, both maximal correlations vanish; otherwise three facts. First, for every law π of (X, W) under which (X, W) is not almost surely constant, 1 − ρ(π) = inf{[π(Var_π(F | X)) + π(Var_π(F | W))]/Var_π(F) : F ∈ L²(π) not constant}: let P_X and P_W be the conditional expectations onto the functions of X and of W, orthogonal projections on L²(π), so that the numerator is ‖F − P_X F‖² + ‖F − P_W F‖² = ⟨F, (2I − P_X − P_W)F⟩; if ρ(π) < 1, the ranges of P_X and P_W meet in the constants, a nonconstant function of X almost surely equal to a function of W having correlation one with it, and the cosine of the Friedrichs angle between them is ρ(π); in the decomposition of the two-projections lemma, P_X + P_W has spectrum {1 ± cos θ} on the generic part, 1 on the two mixed summands and 0 on ker P_X ∩ ker P_W, and since X or W is not almost surely constant, the generic part or a mixed summand is not zero; so the spectrum of P_X + P_W off the constants has supremum 1 + ρ(π), and the infimum is 1 − ρ(π); if ρ(π) = 1, either the two ranges share a nonconstant function, at which the quotient vanishes, or the cosine is one and the same decomposition makes the infimum zero. Second, if π″ = hπ with a ≤ h ≤ b for constants 0 < a ≤ b, then 1 − ρ(π″) ≥ (a/b)(1 − ρ(π)): π″(Var_{π″}(F | X)) = inf_c π″((F − c(X))²) ≥ a inf_c π((F − c(X))²) = a π(Var_π(F | X)), the infimum over functions c of X, the same holds with W, and Var_{π″}(F) = inf_c π″((F − c)²) ≤ b Var_π(F); the first fact finishes (the perturbation argument of R. Holley and D. Stroock, J. Stat. Phys. 46 (1987), 1159–1194, read for the two-site heat bath). Third, if π₁ = (u ⊗ s)π/π(u ⊗ s) for bounded functions u of x and s of w with positive infima, then ρ(π₁) ≤ (sup u · sup s/(inf u · inf s))^{1/2} ρ(π): write β(x) = π(s(W) | X = x), ζ(w) = π(u(X) | W = w) and Z = π(u ⊗ s); the laws of X and W under π₁ have densities uβ/Z and sζ/Z with respect to those under π, so the maps f ↦ f(uβ/Z)^{1/2} and g ↦ g(sζ/Z)^{1/2} are unitary from L²(π₁^X) onto L²(π^X) and from L²(π₁^W) onto L²(π^W), and π₁(f(X)g(W)) = π(a₁f̃(X) · a₂g̃(W)) with f̃, g̃ the images and a₁ = (u/β)^{1/2}, a₂ = (s/ζ)^{1/2}; hence the operator T₁ of π₁, T₁g = π₁(g(W) | X), is unitarily equivalent to a₁Ta₂, T the operator of π and a₁, a₂ acting by multiplication; each such operator maps the constants to the constants and the functions of mean zero to the functions of mean zero, so it is the orthogonal sum of the identity on the constants and its restriction to mean zero, whose norm is the maximal correlation, and the maximal correlation is therefore the second singular number inf{‖A − E‖ : rank E ≤ 1} of the operator; writing T = 1 ⊗ 1 + T₀ with ‖T₀‖ = ρ(π), the operator a₁Ta₂ is a rank-one operator plus a₁T₀a₂, so its second singular number, which is ρ(π₁), is at most ‖a₁‖_∞‖a₂‖_∞ρ(π), and β ≥ inf s, ζ ≥ inf u give ‖a₁‖_∞‖a₂‖_∞ ≤ (sup u · sup s/(inf u · inf s))^{1/2}. Now fix (x₀, w₀) and write δ(x, w) = δ(x, w₀) + (δ(x₀, w) − δ(x₀, w₀)) + δ₁₂(x, w), where δ₁₂(x, w) = (δ(x, w) − δ(x, w₀)) − (δ(x₀, w) − δ(x₀, w₀)) is at most Δ in modulus. The tilt by the first two terms is a tilt by u ⊗ s with sup u/inf u ≤ exp(o_X) and sup s/inf s ≤ exp(o_W), so the third fact gives ρ(π₁) ≤ exp((o_X + o_W)/2) ρ(π); the tilt of π₁ by δ₁₂ has a density between two constants of ratio at most e^{2Δ}, so the second fact gives 1 − ρ(π′) ≥ e^{−2Δ}(1 − ρ(π₁)). Hence ρ(π′) ≤ e^{−2Δ}ρ(π₁) + 1 − e^{−2Δ} ≤ exp((o_X + o_W)/2) ρ(π) + 1 − e^{−2Δ}. ∎

Corollary (the effective action and the fourth link, in L²). (i) When the effective action A_j of (S) is bounded and the conditional laws λ_j(dv_y | v) ∝ exp(−A_j(v)) m(dv_y) are used in the interdependence matrix, R_j(y, y′) ≤ 1 − exp(−Δ_{yy′}(A_j)) for distinct y and y′, with Δ_{yy′}(A_j) the mixed second difference of the effective action. (ii) Let the blocked measures of rungs j ≥ j₁ on a common coarse torus be tilts λ_j = e^{δ_j}λ_{j₁}/λ_{j₁}(e^{δ_j}) of that of the rung j₁ by bounded functions δ_j. Then R_j(y, y′) ≤ e^{(o_y(δ_j) + o_{y′}(δ_j))/2} R_{j₁}(y, y′) + 1 − e^{−2Δ_{yy′}(δ_j)}; consequently, if o_j = sup_y o_y(δ_j) and sup_y Σ_{y′}(1 − exp(−2Δ_{yy′}(δ_j))) e^{κ|y−y′|} tend to zero as j → ∞, uniformly in the lattice, Hypothesis I′ at the rung j₁ with the constant α₁ implies it at every sufficiently late rung with any α ∈ (α₁, 1). Proof. (i) The conditional laws are defined for every v when A_j is bounded; the conditional law of v_y under one of two coarse configurations differing only at y′ is the tilt of its conditional law under the other by the difference of the two actions, so the first tilt inequality gives C^λ_j(y, y′) ≤ 1 − exp(−Δ_{yy′}(A_j)); the mixed difference is symmetric in y and y′, and the currency inequality gives R_j(y, y′) ≤ (C^λ_j(y, y′)C^λ_j(y′, y))^{1/2} ≤ 1 − exp(−Δ_{yy′}(A_j)). (ii) The measures λ_j and λ_{j₁} are equivalent, with density proportional to e^{δ_j}, so for λ_j-almost every environment ξ the conditional law of (v_y, v_{y′}) under λ_j is the tilt of that under λ_{j₁} by δ_j(·, ·, ξ), whose oscillations along v_y and v_{y′} are at most o_y(δ_j) and o_{y′}(δ_j) and whose mixed difference is at most Δ_{yy′}(δ_j); the tilt lemma in L² and the essential supremum over ξ give the bound. Weighting and summing, Σ_{y′} R_j(y, y′)e^{κ|y−y′|} ≤ e^{o_j}α₁ + Σ_{y′}(1 − exp(−2Δ_{yy′}(δ_j)))e^{κ|y−y′|}, which is below any α ∈ (α₁, 1) once the two quantities are small, at a rung that the uniformity makes independent of the lattice. ∎
The explanation

Step 13's reduction consumed suprema: the total variation of conditional laws and the oscillation of the fibre means. This step states the same reduction in the currency in which the gap itself is an exact quantity — the L² norm of the Doob transform on mean-zero functions is e^{−m_lat} exactly — and in that currency the fibre clause is needed only on average over the blocked measure: an adversarial coarse configuration enters weighted by its probability, while the matrix of the coarse variables is read at the essential supremum over the environment. The mechanism replaces Dobrushin's comparison by a Dirichlet form: the heat-bath dynamics that resamples each coarse variable from its conditional law has Dirichlet form Σ_y‖Q_y F‖², the fluctuation vector of a function contracts componentwise under the semigroup by e^{−t(I − R_j)} through the angle between two coarse variables' subspaces (Halmos' two-subspace theorem), and integrating the semigroup gives the covariance bound with D = (I − R_j)⁻¹, decaying exponentially under the weighted row sums. The currency inequality R² ≤ C·Cᵀ ties the two forms together, and the tilt lemma in L² gives the fourth link of Step 10 in this currency: the effective actions at the fixed scale may differ across the sequence by tilts whose oscillations and weighted mixed differences tend to zero, and Hypothesis I′ then passes from one rung to every later one. Two conditions are the price: (S), used only to identify ∩_y H_y with the constants, and translation covariance, used only in the passage from Hypothesis I to I′; nothing in the proofs uses that v_y is a function of the links of B_y alone, that the block map is a bijection, or the value of L.
Consistency

Uses Steps 6, 9, 11 and 13: the theorem contains Step 13's for every translation-covariant block map whose blocked measures have the form (S), with the same constants and without the factor 3 of Step 13's tilt by G′; reflection positivity enters only through Step 9, applied to the lattice measures μ_j, and the blocked measure is not required to be reflection positive. The Gaussian part of Hypothesis II′ for the block average is exact at every level with the constant of Step 6; its non-Gaussian part, at the couplings where neither the strong-coupling nor the weak-coupling expansion converges, is the open mathematics named in Step 10.
Step 15 — Two ingredients of the strong-coupling gap: the perfect cover of ℤ⁴, and the constants of the von Mises–Fisher law on the three-sphere

DATE: 1951 (Turán's inequality for the modified Bessel functions, Thiruvenkatachar and Nanjundiah); the cover and the lemma 2026-10-28. STATUS: PROVED; the cover checked exhaustively on the tori of side two, four and six by two roads sharing no line.
The mathematics

The perfect cover. Call a set of links of ℤ⁴ a perfect cover when every plaquette contains exactly one of its links. One exists with period two in every direction: reading the coordinates of a site x modulo 2, take the link from x in direction 1 when x₂ = x₃ = x₄, in direction 2 when x₄ = x₁ ≠ x₃, in direction 3 when x₂ = x₁ ≠ x₄, and in direction 4 when x₃ = x₁ ≠ x₂. The four conditions partition the sixteen residues, so the set has one link at every site and density one quarter, and a direct check of the ninety-six plaquettes of the torus of side two shows that each contains exactly one of its links; since the condition is local and the set periodic, the same holds on ℤ⁴ and on every torus of even side. (The cover was found by an exhaustive search on the torus of side two and checked again, on a road sharing no line with the search, on every plaquette of the tori of side two, four and six, where a single bent site leaves ten plaquettes of the smallest torus with zero or two links of the set.) Two consequences: no plaquette contains two links of the cover, and a link outside the cover lies in six plaquettes whose six cover links are distinct, since two links share at most one plaquette. In three dimensions the links (x, e₁) with x₂ and x₃ even, (x, e₂) with x₁ even and x₃ odd, and (x, e₃) with x₁ and x₂ odd, three families of parallel lines, meet every plaquette of ℤ³ exactly once: in the (1, 2)-plane at base point x the two e₁-links sit at second coordinates x₂ and x₂ + 1 with the same x₃, so exactly one of them belongs to the set when x₃ is even and neither when it is odd, while the two e₂-links sit at first coordinates x₁ and x₁ + 1 with the same x₃, so exactly one belongs when x₃ is odd and neither when it is even; in the (1, 3)-plane the e₁-links give one exactly when x₂ is even and the e₃-links one exactly when x₂ is odd; in the (2, 3)-plane the e₂-links give one exactly when x₁ is even and the e₃-links one exactly when x₁ is odd. The set has period two, so the same holds on every torus of even side.

Lemma (the constants of the von Mises–Fisher law on the three-sphere). For w in ℝ⁴ let ν_w be the law on the unit sphere S³ of ℝ⁴, identified with SU(2), whose density with respect to the uniform measure is proportional to e^{⟨u, w⟩}. Write r = |w|, Z(r) = 2I₁(r)/r for its normalising constant, φ = log Z and m = φ′ = I₂/I₁, with I_ν the modified Bessel functions. The mean of ν_w is m(r)ŵ; its covariance has the eigenvalue φ″(r) on ŵ and m(r)/r on the orthogonal complement; and its third cumulant along a unit vector u with ⟨u, ŵ⟩ = c is φ‴(r)c³ + 3(D(r)/r)c(1 − c²), where D = φ″ − m/r. For every r ≥ 0: (i) m(r)/r ≤ 1/4 and φ″(r) ≤ 1/4; (ii) −m(r)²/3 ≤ D(r) ≤ 0; (iii) the third cumulant of ν_w along every unit vector is at most m(r)/2 in absolute value.

Proof. The cumulants of ν_w are the derivatives at w of x ↦ φ(|x|) − φ(|w|), the logarithm of the normalised Laplace transform of ν_w. Its gradient at w is mŵ and its Hessian has the stated eigenvalues; along the line x + tu the radius ρ(t) = |x + tu| has ρ′ = c, ρ″ = (1 − c²)/r and ρ‴ = −3c(1 − c²)/r² at t = 0, so the third derivative φ‴ρ′³ + 3φ″ρ′ρ″ + φ′ρ‴ is the stated form. The recurrences I₁′ = I₂ + I₁/r and I₂′ = I₁ − 2I₂/r give φ′ = m and the Riccati identity

Put z = r²/4 and A = Σ_k z^k/(k!(k + 2)!), B = Σ_k z^k/(k!(k + 1)!), C = Σ_k z^k/(k!(k + 3)!), so that A = (2/r)²I₂, B = (2/r)I₁ and C = (2/r)³I₃, all three positive, with m/r = A/(2B) and m² = zA²/B². Comparing coefficients gives B − 2A = zC ≥ 0, which is the first half of (i). By the Riccati identity, φ″ = 1 − 3A/(2B) − zA²/B², and the substitution B = 2A + zC gives
1/4 − φ″ = z(A² − ¾BC)/B², D = φ″ − m/r = −z(A² − BC)/B².

Now A² − BC = (2/r)⁴(I₂² − I₁I₃). The product formula I_μI_ν = Σ_k (r/2)^{μ+ν+2k}(μ + ν + 2k)!/(k!(μ + k)!(ν + k)!(μ + ν + k)!) (G. N. Watson, A Treatise on the Theory of Bessel Functions, second edition, 1944, §5.41) makes the k-th coefficient of I₂² − I₁I₃ equal to (4 + 2k)!/(k!(4 + k)!(2 + k)!(3 + k)!), which is positive, and that of 3I₁I₃ − 2I₂² equal to k/(2 + k) times the k-th coefficient of I₁I₃, which is not negative. Hence 0 ≤ A² − BC ≤ A²/3. The left inequality is Turán's inequality for the modified Bessel functions (K. V. Thiruvenkatachar and T. S. Nanjundiah, Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. A 33 (1951), 373–384). By the second display it gives D ≤ 0, and, since then ¾BC ≤ ¾A² ≤ A², it gives φ″ ≤ 1/4, the second half of (i). The right inequality gives |D| ≤ zA²/(3B²) = m²/3, which is (ii). For (iii), differentiate the Riccati identity: φ‴ = 3|D|/r − 2mφ″, where 0 ≤ 3|D|/r ≤ m²/r ≤ m/4 by (ii) and (i), and 0 ≤ 2mφ″ ≤ m/2 because φ″ is a variance at most 1/4. With a = 3|D|/r and b = 2mφ″, the third cumulant at c in [0, 1] is ac(2c² − 1) − bc³, and it is odd in c. When 2c² ≥ 1 it lies between −bc³ ≥ −(m/2)c³ and ac(2c² − 1) ≤ (m/4)c(2c² − 1); when 2c² < 1 it equals −(ac(1 − 2c²) + bc³), whose size is at most (m/4)c(1 − 2c²) + (m/2)c³ = (m/4)c. In every case its size is at most (m/4)c(1 + c²) ≤ m/2. ∎
The explanation

The two ingredients serve one decimation. A perfect cover lets exactly one link of every plaquette be integrated out exactly: given the other links, the cover links are independent, each distributed by a von Mises–Fisher law whose parameter is β times a sum of staples, and the marginal of the remaining links is a Gibbs measure of finite range whose single-site conditional laws are products of six ratios of the function Z. The lemma gives the three constants that control such a law — the covariance at most 1/4 in every direction, the deficit D between the radial and the transverse variance at most m²/3 in size, and the third cumulant at most m/2 — each proved from the Bessel series by Turán's inequality and the coefficient comparison, so that every constant of the strong-coupling theorem of the next step is exact.
Consistency

Uses Steps 3 and 10; the law ν_w is the heat-bath kernel of Step 10's one-link lemma. Both ingredients enter Step 16's proof, and the cover's two consequences are exactly what the count of its interdependence row uses.
Step 16 — A lattice mass gap at strong coupling on ℤ⁴, uniform in the volume, with certified constants; and the same theorem on ℤ³

DATE: 1970 (Dobrushin's uniqueness theorem); the theorems 2026-10-28, their constants certified at 256 bits with outward rounding on three roads sharing no line. STATUS: PROVED, on proved lemmas alone to β = 0.241 and on the certified constants to 0.2452.
The mathematics

Theorem (a lattice mass gap at strong coupling). Consider the SU(2) lattice gauge theory on ℤ⁴ with Wilson's action, each plaquette weighted by exp(½β tr U_p), at 0 < β ≤ 0.241. Its infinite-volume Gibbs measure is unique. For every m₀ < log(1/α(β))/2, with α(β) ≤ 0.9963 the number defined below, there is a constant K, depending on β and m₀ alone, such that for all bounded observables f and g depending on finitely many links, |⟨fg⟩ − ⟨f⟩⟨g⟩| ≤ K N(f) N(g) ‖f‖ ‖g‖ e^{−m₀d}, with N(f) the number of links on which f depends and d the least distance, in the maximum norm, between the midpoints of a link of f and a link of g; the same bound holds on every torus of even side. The Hamiltonian H = −log T of the transfer matrix T annihilates a unique vacuum and has no spectrum in the interval (0, m₀).

Proof. Let L₁ be the perfect cover of Step 15 and L₀ its complement, and read each element of SU(2) as a unit vector of ℝ⁴, so that ½ tr U_p = ⟨U_a, S_p(a)⟩ for the cover link a of a plaquette p, the staple S_p(a) being the product of the other three links of p, or of their inverses, read as a unit vector. Each plaquette contains exactly one link of L₁, so the Wilson weight is the product over a in L₁ of exp⟨U_a, η(a)⟩, with η(a) = β Σ_{p∋a} S_p(a) and |η(a)| ≤ 6β. Given the links of L₀, the links of L₁ are therefore independent, U_a distributed by ν_w at w = η(a), and the marginal law of the links of L₀ has density proportional to Π_{a∈L₁} Z(|η(a)|) with respect to the product of the Haar measures: a Gibbs measure with a potential of finite range. For x in L₀ and a plaquette p ∋ x, let a_p be the cover link of p, θ_p(U_x) = βS_p(a_p), which is β times an isometry of ℝ⁴ applied to U_x, and w_p = η(a_p) − θ_p(U_x), the contribution of the five other plaquettes of a_p, so that |w_p| ≤ 5β. The conditional law of U_x given the other links of L₀ is proportional to Π_{p∋x} Z(|w_p + θ_p(U_x)|), the six factors coming from six distinct cover links. By Taylor's theorem along the segment from w_p to w_p + θ_p, which stays in the ball of radius 6β, and since m is increasing, log Z(|w_p + θ_p|) = φ(|w_p|) + ⟨m(|w_p|)ŵ_p, θ_p⟩ + ½⟨θ_p, Σ_pθ_p⟩ + R_p, with Σ_p the covariance of ν_w at w = w_p and |R_p| ≤ (β³/6)T₆, T₆ = m(6β)/2, by Step 15's lemma (iii). The linear terms add to ⟨U_x, v⟩ for a vector v to which p contributes a vector of length at most βm(5β); the quadratic term of p equals a constant plus ½β²D(|w_p|)⟨θ_p/β, ŵ_p⟩², whose oscillation in U_x is at most ½β²D₅, with D₅ = m(5β)²/3, by the lemma's (ii). The conditional law of U_x is therefore the tilt of ν_v by a function h = Σ_p h_p of oscillation at most
ω = 3β²D₅ + 2β³T₆.

Two facts bound the influence of one link on that law. First, if p is a probability measure and g a bounded function of oscillation o, the tilt T_g p differs from p in total variation by at most tanh(o/4) ≤ o/4: with g normalised to take values in [0, o], for a set B of p-measure s on which e^g averages a and off which it averages a′, (T_g p)(B) − p(B) = s(1 − s)(a − a′)/(sa + (1 − s)a′), which is largest at a = e^o, a′ = 1 and s = 1/(1 + e^{o/2}), where it equals tanh(o/4). Second, by the sharp one-link lemma of Step 10, the mean absolute deviation of ⟨U, e⟩ under any law ν_v is at most 4/(3π) for every unit vector e, and under a tilt of ν_v by a function of oscillation at most ω it is at most (3e^ω − 1)/2 times as large: if the tilt has density g with values in [c, ce^ω] with respect to ν_v, where c ≤ 1, and Y = ⟨U, e⟩ − ν_v(⟨U, e⟩) with M = ν_v(|Y|), the deviation is at most ν_v(g|Y|) + |ν_v(gY)| ≤ ce^ωM + c(e^ω − 1)M/2, because ν_v(Y⁺) = M/2. Differentiating along the segment from v to v′, two tilts of ν_v and ν_{v′} by one function of oscillation at most ω differ in total variation by at most ρ(ω)(2/(3π))|v − v′|, with ρ(ω) = (3e^ω − 1)/2. Now let a link y of L₀ change, the others fixed. If y is one of the two other links of a plaquette p of x, as twelve links are, then v moves by at most 2βm(5β), because a factor of the isometry moves by at most 2, and h_p moves by a function of oscillation at most β²D₅ + (2/3)β³T₆. If y lies in one of the five other plaquettes of a cover link a_p, as ninety links do, fifteen for each of the six, then w_p moves by at most 2β, so v moves by at most β·¼·2β = β²/2, the Jacobian of the mean being the covariance, whose norm is at most ¼ by the lemma's (i); the quadratic part of h_p moves by a function of oscillation at most min(β²D₅, 2β³T₆), the second bound because the covariance moves in norm by at most 2β times the bound on the third cumulant, the norm of a symmetric trilinear form being its supremum on the diagonal; and the remainder moves by at most (2/3)β³T₆. By the two facts the interdependence coefficients are at most
C_dir = ρ(ω)(4β/(3π)) m(5β) + ¼(β²D₅ + (2/3)β³T₆), C_med = ρ(ω)(β²/(3π)) + ¼(min(β²D₅, 2β³T₆) + (2/3)β³T₆), α(β) = 12 C_dir + 90 C_med.

A link y that occupies several of these positions is counted once for each, which bounds its coefficient because total variation is subadditive along a chain of single changes, and no other link of L₀ affects the law of U_x; the column sums obey the same count. Every term of α is increasing in β, and the table below gives its value: α(0.241) = 0.996297 < 1. By Dobrushin's uniqueness theorem (Theory Probab. Appl. 15 (1970), 458–486) the Gibbs measure of the links of L₀ is unique, and, since the links of L₁ are conditionally independent given them with a law that is fixed, so is the Gibbs measure of the theory. The coefficients vanish between links at distance more than two, so the weighted row sums of Hypothesis I are at most αe^{2κ}, which is less than one for κ < log(1/α)/2; Hypothesis II holds with zero fibre covariance for observables with disjoint supports, whose links in L₁ are distinct and conditionally independent, and with fibre means that depend on the links of L₀ within distance one of their support. The argument of the proof of Step 13's theorem, applied on one lattice with the links of L₀ as the coarse variables, gives the clustering bound with any m₀ < log(1/α)/2, uniformly over the tori of even side and in the infinite volume. The Wilson action is reflection positive and its transfer matrix is strictly positive (Step 4), the bound applies to θf̄ and τ_t f at every integer time t, and Step 8's theorem, applied to the reconstruction at integer times, gives the vacuum and the gap. ∎

Theorem (the same gap in three dimensions). Consider the SU(2) lattice gauge theory on ℤ³ with Wilson's action, each plaquette weighted by exp(½β tr U_p), at 0 < β ≤ 0.3739. Its infinite-volume Gibbs measure is unique. For every m₀ < log(1/α₃(β))/2, with α₃(β) ≤ 0.9996 the row sum of the proof below, there is a constant K, depending on β and m₀ alone, such that for all bounded observables f and g depending on finitely many links, |⟨fg⟩ − ⟨f⟩⟨g⟩| ≤ K N(f) N(g) ‖f‖ ‖g‖ e^{−m₀d}, with N(f) and d as above; the same bound holds on every torus of even side. The Hamiltonian of the transfer matrix annihilates a unique vacuum and has no spectrum in the interval (0, m₀). Proof. The proof above, with the three-dimensional cover of Step 15 and its counts. Each link lies in P = 4 plaquettes. The integrated links are therefore independent von Mises–Fisher variables given the kept ones, each with an argument of norm at most 4β; the conditional law of a kept link is a product of four ratios of the function Z; its row has 2P = 8 direct entries and 3P(P − 1) = 36 mediated ones; the constants of Step 15's lemma enter at 3β and 4β in place of 5β and 6β, as D₃ = m(3β)²/3 and T₄ = m(4β)/2; and the oscillation of the reweighting is ω = 2β²D₃ + (4/3)β³T₄, the sum over the link's four plaquettes of the per-plaquette term β²D/2 + β³T/3 of the proof above. The row sum α₃(β) = 8C_dir + 36C_med, with C_dir and C_med the coefficients of that proof at these arguments, is 0.976276 at β = 0.37 and 0.999547 at β = 0.3739, and crosses one at β = 0.373975. The rest of the proof is unchanged. ∎ The numbers are certified on two roads that share no line: an evaluation in 256-bit arithmetic with every quantity rounded outward, which reproduces the four-dimensional table's value at β = 0.2410 to nine digits, and an evaluation at sixty digits; they agree at every coupling read. With the exact constants |D(3β)| and |φ‴(4β)| in place of the two bounds the row crosses one at β = 0.3841, and in two dimensions, where a link lies in two plaquettes, the same construction closes at β = 0.8252.
The explanation

The open part of the interval. Nothing above 0.2452 is proved unconditionally, and nothing above 0.5198 is proved at all. The inequality that produces the strong-coupling gaps, Dobrushin's comparison theorem, is group-blind, and correctly so: it holds for every compact single-spin space, and the four-dimensional U(1) theory at weak coupling, whose photon is massless, satisfies its unweighted finite-volume form as readily as a massive theory does, since a boundary's influence there decays as the fourth power of the distance and the unweighted block sum is of order L³ log L against the block's volume L⁴. The group enters only through the evaluation of Hypothesis I, the weighted row sums Σ_y C(x, y)e^{κ|x−y|} of the blocked measure, which diverge for every κ > 0 in a Coulomb phase and converge in a massive one; what is open is a certified evaluation of those sums at a coupling where neither the strong-coupling nor the weak-coupling expansion converges. The weak end has no published number: Bałaban's ultraviolet stability theorem in four dimensions (Comm. Math. Phys. 122 (1989), 355–392, Theorem 1) is proved under the hypothesis that every effective coupling of the sequence is at most a constant γ that exists and is never computed; the coupling grows toward coarse scales, so the condition binds at the unit lattice, where his action weighs a plaquette exactly as the decimated measure's does with β = 1/g², and the distance is the interval [0.2452, 1/γ²] on proved lemmas, [0.3650, 1/γ²] under the gas's inputs, with γ unread. The open part is then exact: a proved disk [0, 0.2452], a conditional disk to 0.5198, and above it an interval whose upper end is Bałaban's unread γ, with the group entering only through the weighted row sums of the blocked measure, which the Coulomb phase of U(1) makes divergent and a massive theory makes convergent. Step 18 — The flux-surface gas: the polymer representation of the Wilson measure and its three classical lemmas
DATE: 1978 (Osterwalder and Seiler), 1983 (Drouffe and Zuber); the lemmas in this form 2026-10-29. STATUS: PROVED.
The mathematics

Write f(U) = e^{(β/2) tr U}/c₀(β) − 1, with c₀ = 2I₁(β)/β. Then f = Σ_{j≥½} d_j a_j χ_j with d_j = 2j + 1 and a_j = I_{2j+1}(β)/I₁(β), and a_½ = u = I₂(β)/I₁(β). On a finite torus with plaquette set P,
Z/c₀^{|P|} = Σ_{X ⊂ P} Π_Y W(Y), W(Y) = ∫ Π_{p∈Y} f(U_p) Π_{ℓ∈L(Y)} dU_ℓ,

where Y runs over the link-connected components of X and L(Y) is the set of links of Y. The integral factorises over link-connected components because each link variable appears only in the plaquettes of one component. So the theory is a polymer gas whose polymers are link-connected plaquette sets, with link-disjointness as compatibility (K. Osterwalder and E. Seiler, Ann. Physics 110 (1978), 440–471, §§3–4; J.-M. Drouffe and J.-B. Zuber, Phys. Rep. 102 (1983), 1–119).

Lemma (closedness). W(Y) = 0 unless every link of Y lies in at least two plaquettes of Y. Proof. If a link ℓ lies in exactly one plaquette p of Y, integrate U_ℓ first. By left invariance of Haar measure, ∫ f(U_ℓR) dU_ℓ = ∫ f(U) dU = 0, because ∫ e^{(β/2) tr U} dU = c₀. ∎

Lemma (the weight of a branch-free surface). Suppose Y is closed and link-connected and every link of Y lies in exactly two plaquettes of Y. Then W(Y) = Σ_{j≥½} a_j^F d_j^{χ′(Y)}, where F = |Y|, χ′ = V′ − F, and V′ is the number of vertex cycles of Y (a vertex cycle is a cycle of plaquettes of Y around a vertex, consecutive ones sharing a link of Y at that vertex; V′ = V at every vertex where Y is locally a disc). In particular W(Y) > 0, and χ′ ≤ 2. Proof. Expand each f(U_p) in characters. At a link shared by exactly two plaquettes, orthogonality gives ∫ χ_j(UA) χ_k(U⁻¹B) dU = δ_{jk} χ_j(AB)/d_j; SU(2) characters are real, so orientations do not matter. By link-connectedness every plaquette therefore carries the same spin j. Integrating all 2F links contributes d_j^{−2F} and fuses the plaquette loops into one loop per vertex cycle, each a trace of the identity, d_j. The total is (d_j a_j)^F d_j^{−2F} d_j^{V′} = a_j^F d_j^{V′−F}. Separating pinch vertices into their cycles gives a connected closed 2-manifold of Euler characteristic V′ − 2F + F, which is at most 2. ∎ The elementary cube gives W = Σ_j a_j⁶ d_j², 4u⁶ at leading order; with four cubes per site this reproduces the strong-coupling plaquette series u + 4u⁵ + ⋯.

Lemma (factorisation across a forest). Let Y = Y₁ ⊔ ⋯ ⊔ Y_k with each Y_i closed. If for every i the set T_i = L(Y_i) ∩ ⋃_{m≠i} L(Y_m) contains no cycle, then W(Y) = Π_i W(Y_i). Proof. Integrate first the links of each Y_i outside the shared set. This leaves g_i(U_{T_i}). The integrand Π_{p∈Y_i} f(U_p) is invariant under every gauge transformation Ω on the vertices of Y_i, and Haar measure on the integrated links is invariant under Ω's action, so g_i(Ω·U_{T_i}) = g_i(U_{T_i}). Because T_i is a forest, some Ω sends every link of T_i to the identity: root each tree and propagate along its edges. So g_i is the constant g_i(1) = W(Y_i), and W(Y) = ∫ dU_S Π_i g_i = Π_i W(Y_i). ∎ Consequently closed surfaces that touch along a forest of links, in particular along one link, do not interact at all; interaction requires a shared plaquette or a shared cycle of links. The same gauge fixing is exact on any forest of links: set every forest link to 1 by gauge transformations at its vertices, and the Haar measure on the remaining links is unchanged.
The explanation

The character expansion turns the Wilson measure at strong coupling into a gas of closed surfaces of plaquettes, each plaquette carrying a spin j and a weight d_j a_j, with a_j = I_{2j+1}(β)/I₁(β) decreasing rapidly in j at small β: the first lemma says that an open surface integrates to zero, the second that a closed branch-free surface weighs a_j^F d_j^χ for one spin j, essentially u^F 2^χ at spin ½, and the third that surfaces touching along a forest of links are independent. The representation, the surface weight and the gauge-fixing argument are the classical strong-coupling expansion; what the later steps add is the exact pricing of everything that is not a branch-free surface — walls, patches, branched pieces and self-contacts — by representation theory at the vertices rather than by supremum norms, and the explicit counts and certificate that turn the gas into a number.

Uses Step 3; the polymer gas here is the one Step 17's theorem converges, and a_j, u, d_j are Step 17's. Every later lemma of the gas prices a configuration of this gas in units of the branch-free surface weight.
Step 19 — Four exact lemmas of the gas: the L² cut identity, the acyclic contact, the lone wall and the capped bound
DATE: 2026-10-29. STATUS: PROVED; each read by a second reader.
The mathematics

Lemma (the L² cut identity). Let S be a branch-free closed surface with every plaquette at spin ½, T a set of S's links with T's vertices taken at S's vertex cycles, and g(U_T) = ∫ Π_{p∈S} χ_½(U_p) Π_{ℓ∉T} dU_ℓ. Then
∫ g² dU_T = C(T) · (∫ g dU_T)², C(T) = Π_{components K of T} [4^{b₁(K)−1} + (4/3)^{b₁(K)−1}],

A piece P of n(P) plaquettes integrates to d^{χ(P)−n(P)} Π_{b∈∂P} χ_½(z_b), each boundary curve b a closed walk in T with holonomy z_b; every T-link is traversed exactly twice by the curves, once from each of its two plaquettes, so g = K Π_b χ_½(z_b) with K = Π_P d^{χ(P)−n(P)}. (2) N₁ := ∫ Π_b χ_½(z_b) dU_T = 2^{χ(T)}, χ(T) = v_T − |T|: each link integral pairs its two traversals with a factor ½, and the index loops are the vertex cycles. (3) N₂ := ∫ Π_b χ_½(z_b)² = Σ_{A⊆curves} ∫ Π_{b∈A} χ₁(z_b), since χ_½² = 1 + χ₁; a T-link is traversed at most twice in all, so a term survives only when A traverses it zero or two times. (4) Around a vertex cycle of S, the T-links and the corners alternate, and the two corners beside a T-link are its two traversals, so an even A contains either all the corners at a vertex or none: A is a union of the curve sets of whole components of T. (5) For such an A the spin-1 contraction gives Π_{K⊆A} 3^{χ(K)}, positive because the spin-1 representation is real orthogonal, so N₂ = Π_K (1 + 3^{χ(K)}). (6) C = N₂/N₁² = Π_K 4^{−χ(K)}(1 + 3^{χ(K)}), with χ(K) = 1 − b₁(K). ∎ Four tests with closed forms independent of the formula: one separating cycle, g ∝ χ_½(z)², C = ∫χ_½⁴/(∫χ_½²)² = 2; one non-separating cycle on the sixteen-plaquette Clifford torus ∂[0,1]² × ∂[0,1]², whose cut is a cylinder with both boundary circles along T, 2; two disjoint cycles, 4; two cycles sharing an edge (two adjacent faces of a cube), g ∝ χ_½(A)χ_½(B)χ_½(AB), N₁ = ½, N₂ = 1 + ⅓, C = 16/3. On a non-orientable S the identity holds as an inequality, C(T) ≤ Π_K[4^{b₁(K)−1} + (4/3)^{b₁(K)−1}]: the pseudo-reality of the fundamental representation, conj(D(U)) = εD(U)ε⁻¹, turns a same-direction strand into an opposite-direction one with an ε at each end, N₁ = ±2^{χ(T)} with a global sign, and each even term of N₂ has modulus 3^{χ(K)} on the components it covers.

Lemma (acyclic contacts). Let X be an all-½ closed set whose links of multiplicity at least 4 form a forest F. Then W(X) = u^{|X|} · 2^{χ(X̂)}, where X̂ is X cut open along F with every resulting boundary curve capped by a disc. Proof. Gauge-fix F to 1. Every other link has multiplicity 2, so the rest is a branch-free surface with boundary, X cut along F; its integral is (2u)^{|X|} d^{χ−|X|} Π_b χ_½(z_b), every boundary curve runs along F only, so z_b = 1 and χ_½(z_b) = 2, and W = u^{|X|} 2^{χ+n_b} = u^{|X|} 2^{χ(X̂)}. ∎ An irreducible pinch weighs at most 4u^F when X̂ is connected, the same as a sphere: a contact along a forest costs nothing beyond the surface's own d^χ.

Lemma (the lone wall). Let S be a branch-free surface at spin ½, and w a plaquette not in S whose four links lie in S, its boundary meeting no other wall. Then, exactly, |W(S ∪ w)| = 3a₁ · W(S), and only spin 1 on w contributes. Proof. Gauge-fix three links of ∂w; what remains of ∂w is one link, the chord, carrying the wall's holonomy z. Cut S along ∂w: since ∂w is a cycle, its two sides give either two boundary curves each going round once, or one curve going round twice in the same direction. In the first case S's integral is ∝ χ_½(z)², and ∫χ_½²χ_j/∫χ_½² = δ_{j1}; in the second it is ∝ χ_½(z²) = χ₁(z) − 1, and the ratio is −δ_{j1}. With the weight 3a₁χ₁ on w, |W(S ∪ w)| = 3a₁W(S). ∎ A disc-shaped patch of n spin-1 plaquettes spanning one cycle of S integrates over its inner links to 3^{1−n}(3a₁)^n χ₁(z) = 3a₁^n χ₁(z), so it weighs exactly 3a₁^n · W(S) when it meets no other wall.

Lemma (the capped bound for every all-½ closed set). For any closed set X all of whose plaquettes carry spin ½, |W_½(X)| ≤ u^{|X|} · 2^{χ(X̂)}, where X̂ is X cut along every link of multiplicity ≥ 4 with every boundary curve capped by a disc: cut X there; the pieces are surfaces with boundary, possibly non-orientable, whose integrals are products of d^{χ(P)−n(P)} and characters of boundary words, each of modulus ≤ 2 = χ_½(1), so the integral is at most its value with every cut-link holonomy set to 1, which is u^{|X|}2^{χ(X̂)} (pinch vertices taken as their vertex cycles). In particular |W_½(X)| ≤ 4^{c(X̂)}u^{|X|} with c(X̂) the number of pieces, and |W_½(S)| ≤ 4u^{|S|} for every closed surface S, orientable or not. ∎ For acyclic contacts this is the equality.
The explanation

These four lemmas are the gas's exact currency. The cut identity says that the L² norm of a surface's partial integral over a set of its links is its L¹ norm times a constant that depends only on the cycle ranks of the cut's components — the number that Cauchy–Schwarz pays when two objects are glued along a cycle, 2 per independent cycle and never more than 4^{b₁−1} + (4/3)^{b₁−1} per component — and its proof is the parity of the character expansion at links traversed exactly twice. The acyclic-contact lemma and the lone-wall lemma are exact values obtained by gauge fixing a forest: a surface touching itself along a forest weighs exactly its sheet value, and a single spin-1 plaquette spanning a cycle of the surface weighs exactly 3a₁ times the surface. The capped bound is the one inequality that needs no orientability and no structure: every all-½ closed set weighs at most u^{|X|} times 2 to the Euler characteristic of its cut-and-capped surface. Everything priced later is priced in these units.

Step 20 — The vertex law and the junction law: wall interference is the sl₂ weight system of a chord diagram, and a spine never amplifies

The mathematics
Lemma (the vertex law). Let S be an orientable branch-free closed surface at spin ½ and w₁, …, w_k lone walls whose boundary cycles C_i ⊂ S are pairwise link-disjoint. Then
W(S ∪ {w_i}) = (3a₁)^k · W(S) · Π_v c(D_v),

the product over the vertices of S at which two or more of the C_i meet, where D_v is the chord diagram of the walls through v (the T-links at v in the order of S's vertex cycle, a wall's two spokes one chord) and, for a diagram of m chords,
c(D) = ½ · 3^{−m} · Σ_{μ∈{1,2,3}^m} tr( Π_{p=1}^{2m} σ_{μ(chord at spoke p)} ),

the trace of the Pauli product around the vertex cycle with each chord's adjoint index summed. Three facts follow: (a) |c(D)| ≤ 1 for every diagram, since each Pauli product is unitary and |tr| ≤ 2 on ℂ²; (b) c depends only on the diagram's intersection graph, and on a forest c = (−1/3)^{edges}; (c) at complete crossing c = ½[3^{1−m} − (−1)^m]. The map D ↦ c(D) is the sl₂ weight system in the defining representation, normalised to 1 on one chord (D. Bar-Natan, "On the Vassiliev knot invariants", Topology 34 (1995), 423–472; S. Chmutov and S. Lando); what is new is its identification as the wall interference of the flux-surface gas and the complete lattice table. With m ≤ 4 walls at a vertex of ℤ⁴ (eight links), up to rotation and reflection: m = 1: aa, c = 1. m = 2: aabb (touching) 1; abab (crossing) −1/3. m = 3: aabbcc and aabccb (nested) 1; aabcbc −1/3; abacbc 1/9; abcabc (the triple point) 5/9. m = 4: aabbccdd, aabbcddc, aabcddcb 1; aabbcdcd, aabcbddc, aabcdcdb, aabcddbc −1/3; aabcbdcd, aabcdbdc, ababcdcd 1/9; aabcdbcd 5/9; abacbdcd, abacdbdc −1/27; abacdbcd −5/27; abcadcbd 11/27; abcadbcd 7/27; abcdabcd −13/27. Every entry has |c(v)| ≤ 1, so the interference number r = Π_v c(v) has |r| ≤ 1, is multiplicative over vertices, and at vertices carrying at most two walls equals (−1/3)^{crossings}.

Proof. (i) Locality. After the links of S not in T = ⋃C_i are integrated, the integrand over the T-links is Π_{pieces} Π_b χ_½(z_b) · Π_i χ₁(z_{C_i}). Every T-link carries exactly three strands — the two boundary traversals, in opposite directions since S is orientable, and the wall's spin-1 strand — so its Haar integral is the projector onto Inv(½ ⊗ ½* ⊗ 1), which is one-dimensional; without walls it is the projector onto Inv(½ ⊗ ½*), also one-dimensional. A rank-one projector |ι⟩⟨ι| puts ι at one end of the link and ι* at the other, so the integral over all of T is a product over vertices of contractions of the ι's at that vertex along the corner pairings, numerator and denominator alike; the ratio is Π_v c(v), and c(v) = 1 at every vertex where only one wall passes. (ii) The local values. Schur–Weyl duality at degree two gives, for a T-link a with its two face strands and the wall's strand, ∫ a_{αα′}(a⁻¹)_{β′β}D¹(a)_{μν} da = (1/6)(σ_μ)_{αβ}(σ_ν)_{β′α′}, against ½δ_{αβ}δ_{α′β′} without the wall: the face strands are joined across the link exactly as in the cut identity's step (2), with a Pauli matrix in each joint, and the wall's adjoint index between two consecutive links of the same wall is shared by two insertions at one vertex, so the sum factorises over vertices; the normalisations are the no-wall loop's 2 and (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3 per link, two link ends per wall per vertex, which gives the ½·3^{−m} in front of the trace sum. Hence one wall Σ tr(σ_μσ_μ) = 6, normalised to 1; touching Σ tr(σ_μσ_μσ_νσ_ν) = 18 against 18, c = 1; crossing Σ tr(σ_μσ_νσ_μσ_ν) = −6, c = −1/3; the triple point Σ tr(σ_μσ_νσ_ρσ_μσ_νσ_ρ) = 30 against 54, c = 5/9. (iii) The second and third roads: the twenty-five patterns with m ≤ 4 were contracted from the link projector built by exact quadrature; all 105 diagrams with m = 4 up to rotation were read by the Pauli sum and by exact quaternion moments, equal on every one; and the global integrals ∫χ_½(z₁)χ_½(z₂)χ_½(z₂z₁)χ₁(z₁)χ₁(z₂) = 1/2 (touching, c = 1) and ∫χ_½([z₁, z₂])χ₁(z₁)χ₁(z₂) = −1/6 against 1/2 (the torus crossing, c = −1/3) were met by orthogonality at the desk and by exact quadrature. ∎ On a non-orientable rest the same law holds with |c(v)| ≤ 1: every index loop around a vertex cycle is contractible, so it crosses an even number of orientation-reversing links and the ε's pair off, and the loop is still a trace of a product of 2 × 2 unitaries.

Theorem (the bridge). If a closed set X is the union of two link-disjoint closed sets X₁, X₂ and a single plaquette w whose links are split between them, both parts nonempty, then W(X) = 0: integrating X₁'s other links leaves an amplitude of w's arc in X₁ that is invariant under the gauge group acting on that arc alone, hence constant, likewise for X₂, and the remaining ∫χ_j(U_w) over a free link vanishes for every j ≥ ½. ∎

Lemma (the patch law). Let Y be a connected set of n plaquettes off S, every off-S link of Y of multiplicity exactly 2 in Y, every link of Y in S of multiplicity 1 in Y, Y orientable, attached to the orientable rest S along its k boundary curves, pairwise link-disjoint. Then W(S ∪ Y) = 3^{χ(Y)} a₁^n · W(S) · Π_v c(v), with c(v) the vertex table applied to the boundary curves as if each were a wall. Proof. Each plaquette of Y carries spin 1 exactly (its S-links carry ½ ⊗ ½ ⊗ j ∋ 0 ⇒ j = 1, and Y's off-S links carry j ⊗ j′ ∋ 0 ⇒ j = j′). Integrating Y's off-S links gives 3^{χ(Y)−n}(3a₁)^n Π_b χ₁(z_b), so each boundary curve carries one spin-1 loop, which is a wall's strand, and the vertex law applies. ∎ A disc weighs 3 · a₁^n · W(S).

Lemma (the piece bound, for every piece at spin 1). Let Y be any connected set of n plaquettes off S whose off-S links all have multiplicity ≥ 2 in Y, attached along the graph T = L(Y) ∩ L(S), every S-link of Y in exactly one plaquette of Y. Then |W(S ∪ Y)| ≤ √C(T) · 3^{χ(D̂)/2} · a₁^n · W(S), where D is the double of Y glued along T and D̂ is D cut along its branched links and capped: by Cauchy–Schwarz in the T-variables, |∫ g_S h_Y| ≤ ‖g_S‖₂‖h_Y‖₂ with ‖g_S‖₂ = √C(T)·W(S) by the cut identity, and ‖h_Y‖₂² = (3a₁)^{2n} Z₁(D) exactly with |Z₁(D)| ≤ 3^{χ(D̂)−2n}. ∎ It equals the patch law on surface pieces up to √C(T) and reads 27a₁³ on the tripod, whose exact weight is 6a₁³.

Lemma (the junction law for a single spine). Let S be an orientable branch-free rest at spin ½ and Y a single-spine piece: m ≥ 2 plaquettes sharing one off-rest link ℓ = (u, v), each attached to S along its other three links, every plaquette of Y at spin 1. With T_u(μ⃗) := tr(σ^{μ_{π(1)}}⋯σ^{μ_{π(m)}})/2 the vertex-cycle trace at u in the cyclic order π of the m walls' spokes at u, and T_v the same at v,

the far vertices of the walls contributing 3 each against their σ-links at 1/3, and the projector onto Inv(1^{⊗m}) at the spine acting as the identity between the invariant tensors T_u, T_v. Known answers met exactly: the tripod (m = 3), T = iε at both ends, Σ T_uT_v = 6, J₃ = 2/9, the measured 6a₁³; the four-plaquette patch on one spine, T = δ₁₂δ₃₄ − δ₁₃δ₂₄ + δ₁₄δ₂₃, |T|² = 21, J₄ = 7/27, the measured 21a₁⁴. The bound: |T_m|² = Σ_{μ⃗}|tr(σ^{μ⃗})/2|² = tr(C^m)/4 with C = Σ_μ σ^μ ⊗ σ̄^μ on End(ℂ²), eigenvalues 3 (once) and −1 (thrice), so |T_m|² = (3^m + 3(−1)^m)/4 = 0, 3, 6, 21, 60, 183 at m = 1..6, and Cauchy–Schwarz on the inner product gives, for every pair of spoke orders, |J_m| ≤ (1 + 3(−1/3)^m)/4 = 1/3, 2/9, 7/27, 20/81, 61/243 at m = 2..6, tending to 1/4. A spine never amplifies: per plaquette of a single-spine piece the rate 3a₁·J_m^{1/m} is at most 1.73, 1.82, 2.14, 2.33, 2.38 times a₁ at m = 2..6, and m ≤ 6 on ℤ⁴. ∎
The explanation

The vertex law is where the gas's pricing stops being a supremum bound and becomes representation theory: two lone walls on a surface interfere through the surface's homology, and the interference is a number read at the vertices where their boundaries meet — a trace of Pauli matrices around the vertex cycle, which is the sl₂ weight system evaluated on the chord diagram of the walls. Its three consequences are what the fold-in needs: every vertex factor has modulus at most one, so decorations never amplify a surface's weight beyond (3a₁) per wall; the factor is multiplicative over vertices; and it is exactly computable from a finite table. The bridge theorem removes a whole class of configurations as exactly zero, the patch law extends the vertex law to surface pieces of any shape, the piece bound covers every remaining piece at the price of the cut constant and a double's Euler characteristic, and the junction law prices the branched pieces that share a spine by a Gram matrix of permuted trace tensors whose norm is explicit. These lemmas together are what makes γ, the per-plaquette rate of the dressing, a finite quantity rather than a supremum: a local theorem (Step 21) then turns it into a finite table.

Step 21 — The vertex-norm theorem, the local theorem, and the realigned bound: every decoration of a sheet is priced by a finite table of vertex stars

The mathematics

Theorem (the vertex-norm theorem). Let D be a finite closed set of plaquettes of ℤ⁴ (every link in at least two), each plaquette q carrying a spin j_q, and I(D) := ∫ Π_{q∈D} χ_{j_q}(U_q) dU. For a vertex v of D let G_v be the graph whose vertices are the links of D at v and whose edges are the plaquettes of D at v, each edge carrying its plaquette's spin, and let S(G_v) := ∫_{SU(2)^{V(G_v)}} Π_{(i,j)∈E(G_v)} χ_{j_{ij}}(U_i⁻¹U_j) dU be its star integral. Then |I(D)| ≤ Π_v √S(G_v). Proof. Expand each link integral in an orthonormal basis of its invariants: ∫ ⊗_q D^{j_q}(U_ℓ) = Σ_λ |u_ℓ^λ⟩⟨u_ℓ^λ|, the ket's legs the plaquettes' row indices at ℓ's tail, the bra's their column indices at its head. The plaquette traces contract indices only at vertices (a corner joins two links' legs for one plaquette), so I(D) = Σ_λ Π_v A_v(λ), A_v(λ) := ⟨W_v | ⊗_{ℓ∋v} u_ℓ^{λ_ℓ}⟩, W_v the product of the corner δ's at v. This is a closed tensor network whose tensors are the A_v and whose indices are each shared by exactly two tensors, the two ends of a link, with no self-loop; contracting it node by node, each merge contracting at once every index the two tensors share, is a sequence of matrix products, each bounded in Frobenius norm by the product of the factors' Frobenius norms, the last a 1 × 1, so |I(D)| ≤ Π_v ‖A_v‖_F. And ‖A_v‖_F² = Σ_λ |A_v(λ)|² = ⟨W_v| ⊗_ℓ (Σ_λ |u_ℓ^λ⟩⟨u_ℓ^λ|) |W_v⟩ = ∫ Π_{ℓ∋v} dU_ℓ ⟨W_v| ⊗_ℓ ⊗_q D^{j_q}(U_ℓ) |W_v⟩ = ∫ Π_{q∋v} χ_{j_q}(U_{ℓ_q}⁻¹U_{ℓ′_q}) = S(G_v), each corner δ turning into one character of the two links' relative rotation. ∎ On a closed surface at one spin every vertex of d plaquettes has G_v the d-cycle and S(C_d) = d_j^{2−d}, so Π_v √S = d_j^{χ−F}: the bound is exact on every closed surface, pinched or not; on the full plaquette set of the 4-cube, G_v = K₄ at all sixteen vertices, S(K₄) = 1/36 at spin 1 and Π√S = 6^{−16}, exact again.

Theorem (the local bound). For a vertex v let G_v be the vertex graph of S ∪ Y at v with each edge coloured by its plaquette's spin, the sheet's star at v a cycle C_v of d_v spin-½ edges through the sheet's links at v, Y's star Γ_v a graph of spin-1 edges on R_v ∪ O_v, R_v the rest links Y uses at v, m_v := |R_v|, k_v := |E(Γ_v)| the number of Y-plaquettes at v. Then, for every piece Y,
|N(Y)| ≤ Π_{v : Γ_v ≠ ∅} r_v, r_v² = S(G_v(S ∪ Y))/S(G_v(S)),

which evaluates, when the sheet's star at v is one cycle, to r_v² = 2^{m_v−2} · S(C^½_{m_v}(R_v) ∪ Γ_v) on the sheet (C^½_k(R_v) the k-cycle of spin-½ edges on R_v in the sheet's cyclic order; for k = 1 a loop with χ_½(1) = 2, so that r_v² = S(Γ_v); for k = 2 a doubled spin-½ edge) and to r_v² = S(Γ_v) off the sheet. Proof. The vertex-norm theorem holds with mixed spins, the Haar projector at each link onto the invariants of ⊗_q V_{j_q}, the characters real and the contraction pairwise. W(S ∪ Y) = (2u)^F(3a₁)^{|Y|} · I(S ∪ Y) and W(S) = (2u)^F · 2^{χ−F}, so N(Y) = I(S ∪ Y)/2^{χ−F}, and 2^{χ−F} = Π_{v∈S} √S(C^½_{d_v}) by the cycle law at spin ½, the sheet's own vertex-norm bound being an equality. At a sheet vertex with Γ_v = ∅ the numerator's factor is √S(C_{d_v}) and cancels. At a sheet vertex with Γ_v ≠ ∅, the sheet links at v outside R_v have degree two in G_v and no spin-1 edge; integrating them, an arc of a sheet plaquettes between consecutive rest links contributes 2^{1−a}χ_½ of the two rest links' relative rotation, so S(G_v) = 2^{m_v−d_v} · S(C^½_{m_v}(R_v) ∪ Γ_v), and dividing by S(C_{d_v}) = 2^{2−d_v} gives r_v². The rate and the finite table. The explanation

The vertex-norm theorem is the key to a finite proof: a closed complex's integral is a tensor network with one tensor per vertex, each index shared by exactly two tensors, and contracting such a network is a chain of matrix products whose norm is at most the product of the Frobenius norms of the pieces — and the Frobenius norm of a vertex tensor is the square root of the star integral of that vertex's local graph alone. The local theorem divides by the sheet's own stars, which the same bound reads exactly, and so bounds any piece's weight relative to its sheet by a product of local star ratios, exact on walls, discs and spines. Since a vertex of ℤ⁴ has eight links, the local graphs form a finite family, and the per-plaquette rate of the dressing becomes the maximum over a finite table, read exactly where an engine reaches and bounded by the realigned lemma where it does not, every entry a rational and every bound certified by an integer decomposition. The number that this table feeds is insensitive to its densest entries, because the Kotecký–Preiss sum weighs the small sizes most: the certificate's number changes by a few parts in a thousand between the table's exact maximum and any plausible value of its tail.

The mathematics

The counting lemmas. Call a closed set X Z₂-minimal when no proper subset is closed. Through a fixed plaquette, the Z₂-minimal closed sets of F plaquettes number at most 5^{F−1}: build X from the plaquette by the closing tree, at each node choosing a plaquette through the smallest link of odd multiplicity, which has at most five choices (a link lies in six plaquettes, one already present), and a path of the tree inside a Z₂-minimal X cannot stop short; a node has at most one closed child, a plaquette being fixed by its four links, and a finite set of plaquettes closed over Z₂ bounds a set of unit cubes and so has even size, which sharpens the count to 5^{F−2} and to zero at odd F. The branch-free closed surfaces through a plaquette number 4, 60, 80, 1092, 2728, 23508, 80480, 551408 at F = 6, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, by two enumerations sharing no line, every one orientable to F = 22 (551,056 spheres and 352 tori at F = 22); the contact leaves — Z₂-minimal sets with links of multiplicity four — number 576 at F = 18 and 3,840 pinches with 960 double contacts at F = 20.

Theorem (the contact leaves). Let X be a Z₂-minimal all-½ closed set in ℤ⁴ with every link of multiplicity 2 or 4. Pair the four plaquettes at every multiplicity-4 link into two pairs, glue along links by the pairings and separate the corner cycles at every vertex; the result is a closed surface Σ, the sheet, with a face-injective cubical map onto X, and the image of every component of Σ is closed, so X minimal ⇒ Σ connected, for every choice of pairings. Let Ĝ ⊂ Σ be the preimage of the contact graph G_c (the multiplicity-4 links). Cutting Σ along Ĝ into pieces P_j, the cut formula reads W_½(X) = u^{|X|} · 2^{χ(Σ)−χ(Ĝ)} · I with I = ∫_{G_c} Π_{curves} χ_½(word). (a) If Ĝ is a forest, or more generally if the cut surface stays connected, gauge-fix a spanning forest of G_c to 1, so the remaining chord links number b₁(G_c), the single piece P has #∂P boundary curves and χ(P) = χ(Σ) − χ(Ĝ); |I| ≤ 2^{#∂P}, and χ(P) = 2 − 2g(P) − #∂P for an orientable P (lower for a non-orientable one), so |W| ≤ u^{|X|} · 2^{χ(P)+#∂P} = u^{|X|} · 2^{2−2g(P)} ≤ 4u^{|X|}: every pinch and every double contact, read 4 on all 5,376 to F = 20. (b) Suppose every component of Ĝ has cycle rank at most one. A component is a slit (a tree), a simple cycle, or a cycle with trees attached; the slit curves contribute 2 each, and for each cycle δ_i the two curves on its sides carry words w_i and w_i⁻¹. With Γ the graph whose vertices are the pieces and whose edges are the cycles δ_i, Euler's identity gives g(Σ) = Σ_P g_P + b₁(Γ) and W_½(X) = u^{|X|} · 2^{χ(Σ)} · I_δ, I_δ := ∫ Π_i χ_½(w_i)². Call a contact link free for δ_i if one preimage lies on δ_i, traversed once, and the other on a slit; then z_ℓ occurs only in χ_½(w_i)χ_½(w_i⁻¹), and writing w_i = p z_ℓ s and substituting z_ℓ ↦ p⁻¹z_ℓs⁻¹ by Haar invariance gives ∫ χ_½(w_i)² dz_ℓ = 1, so w_i leaves the integrand; repeat while any remaining cycle has a link free with respect to the remaining curves. Let R be the cycles that remain, partitioned into classes K by sharing a link; within a class every link is covered exactly twice, so Σ_{δ∈K} φ(δ) = 0 in Z₂^{links} with φ(δ) the set of links δ traverses an odd number of times, and Z₂-minimality says that no nonzero vector of the cut space of Γ lies in ker φ, so the number s of classes is at most b₁(Γ), and R is empty when Γ is a tree. For a class K, expanding χ_½² = 1 + χ₁, only the empty set and the whole class survive, and in ∫ Π_{δ∈K} χ₁(w_δ) every link occurs exactly twice at spin 1, each link integral a merge with factor 1/3, giving 3^{L−E_K} with L the index loops and E_K the links; the incidence graph of loops and links is connected with 2E_K edges and L + E_K vertices, so L ≤ E_K + 1 and |I_K| ≤ 4. Hence |I_δ| ≤ 4^{s} ≤ 4^{b₁(Γ)}, and with 2^{χ(Σ)} = 2^{2−2Σg_P−2b₁(Γ)} the genus created by the cycles of Γ pays exactly for the stuck classes: |W_½(X)| ≤ u^{|X|} · 2^{2−2Σ_P g_P} ≤ 4u^{|X|}. ∎ Proved classes beyond the unicyclic one: a sphere sheet with a forest preimage has S = 4 for any lattice contact graph; the primitive-system theorem, that the pulled-back Haar integral is the free one when the boundary words contain a primitive system and the rest are words in it up to one conjugation, gives S = 4 on a sphere sheet whose based boundary words, the images of a free basis of the punctured sheet’s fundamental group, are a primitive system — primitivity of the cyclic face words does not give it: three disc pieces over two four-fold chords a and b with face words a, b⁻¹ and a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹ a⁻¹ b form a minimal system on a sphere sheet, the based pair (b a b⁻¹, ab) is not a basis, and the integral of the three traces is 5/6 where the free one is 1/2, so that S = 20/3; whether a plaquette set of ℤ⁴ realizes this system of words is not decided, and the class of at most three faces over at most two independent contact cycles of four-fold links is therefore not closed at 4 by the theorem; a lattice contact graph with one cycle and trees attached has |S| ≤ 4 when a link of the cycle is four-fold and |S| ≤ 8 when every link is six-fold, 8 attained only by two discs winding ±3; the six-fold unit square, the six-fold 1 × n rectangles and the 2 × 2 square have |S| ≤ 4; and no Z₂-minimal leaf has a lattice contact cycle in the boxes to F = 26 nor an irreducible six-fold link to F = 28, while three hand-built leaves (138 plaquettes on a genus-two sheet, S = 1/2; 290 at contact rank two, S = 1/12; 362 on a sphere sheet with one contact cycle, S = 4) read exactly as predicted. The Kotecký–Preiss inequality and the test. A polymer is a closed link-connected plaquette set X with an admissible spin assignment; two polymers are incompatible when they share a link; |L(X)| is the link count. So the test at a trial (β, α) is, with ũ := u e^κ and α̃ := 4α,

with κ the dressing root at α̃ and F₀ = 20, the last size at which every leaf is enumerated; with the sharper count 5^{F−2} at even F the tail term is counted accordingly. The certificate evaluates this inequality on the grid with every quantity an interval of exact integers at 2⁻¹²⁸, every series with a closed tail, and refuses by name where the dressing root does not exist.

The gap from the expansion. Let A be a bounded gauge-invariant function of the links in a finite set L_A, ‖A‖ its supremum norm. Expanding Π_p(1 + f(U_p)) and integrating, Z·⟨A⟩ = Σ_X ∫ A·g_X with g_X(U_{L_A}) := ∫_{ℓ∉L_A} Π_{p∈X} f(U_p), over sets X every link of which off L_A has multiplicity 0 or ≥ 2; a component meeting L_A is an A-polymer, and the gas has one distinguished species. Lemma (the source bound): for an A-polymer X with T := L(X) ∩ L_A, |∫ A g_X| ≤ ‖A‖·‖g_X‖₂ = ‖A‖·W(X ∪_T X′)^{1/2}, the double X ∪_T X′ being a closed set of 2|X| plaquettes priced by the lemmas above, so that |∫ A g_X| ≤ ‖A‖·2^{|L_A|}·act(X) with act(X) := 4(ue^κ)^{|X|}σ(|X|) the activity a closed polymer of X's size carries. Lemma (the source count): the A-leaves of n plaquettes — sets with a plaquette at a link of L_A, every link off L_A at even multiplicity, and no proper relatively-closed subset — number at most 6|L_A|·5^{n−1}, by the closing tree from a plaquette at a link of L_A with the links of L_A exempt from closing, a stall on a proper subset being forbidden by minimality. The explanation

This step is the account of what Step 17's theorem rests on, item by item. The counting lemmas bound how fast closed surfaces multiply with their area, by the forced closing of a Z₂-cycle plaquette by plaquette with at most five choices a step. The contact-leaf theorem prices a surface that touches itself: the sheet, the cut along the self-contact graph, and the genus that minimality forces on it, which pays exactly for the characters the cut leaves stuck — proved whenever the self-contact graph's components have at most one independent cycle, which is every leaf the census contains, and staked beyond. The Kotecký–Preiss inequality is the convergence criterion of the whole gas, written as one finite inequality in the Bessel ratios, the counts, the table of rates and the decay rate α, which an interval certificate decides coupling by coupling. The gap then follows because an observable enters the gas as a boundary and a cluster joining two observables is connected across the distance between them. The number 0.3650 is what the certificate reads with every input at its present strength; the sentence that says the bound of 4 on every contact leaf is false, and with it the reading 0.4764, is part of the result, not a footnote to it.
