Step 23 — The window theorem as the one open link, and its exact form: the exit budget, the relative content, and the exit condition as a certificate

DATE: 2026-11-01. STATUS: the lemma PROVED as a reduction whose content is two numbers; the budget CERTIFIED; the pricing-comparison lemma read by a second reader, its corrections taken; the first blocking step from β = 2.2 REFUSED by the certificate at every datum read.
The mathematics

The free choice. The physical scale a_c of Step 13's reduction is ours to choose on the construction's sequence. Blocking past the correlation length carries the effective Wilson coupling into the strong-coupling region where Step 17's expansion (β ≤ β*) and Step 16's comparison (β ≤ 0.2452) are theorems, so the inequality that must hold uniformly in the cutoff is read at the exit of the crossover, where it is a stability statement about a convergent expansion and not a supremum criterion at the crossover coupling itself.

The lemma (the scale-uniform inequality). Fix a_c so that the blocked Wilson coupling there is β_c ≤ β*, and write the blocked action at a_c as Wilson(β_c) + Σ_C δ_C, the sum over connected plaquette sets C of its multi-plaquette couplings; a single-plaquette correction is a class function and is absorbed into the one-plaquette weight, whose character coefficients a′_j are then no longer Bessel ratios. Define the exit budget ε(β_c) as the largest per-plaquette tilt under which the gas's Kotecký–Preiss inequality at β_c still holds with the rate α, every polymer's activity multiplied by e^{ε|X|}. If the content of the couplings lies under the budget uniformly along the sequence, the blocked measure at a_c has a convergent polymer expansion with the rate α for every cutoff, which is Hypothesis I in the form Step 13's theorem consumes. The budget is computable: with every character coefficient multiplied by e^{tilt} in directed rounding and every polymer's weight by e^{tilt·|X|}, the certificate of Step 22 decides the tilted inequality, and reads, with its tail at the contact-leaf bound that Step 17 shows false — so that these are the budgets of that certificate, upper marks for the budgets with the all-spin tail, whose region ends at 0.3650 — at α = 0.001 and 0.004: ε = 2.32 / 2.36 at β = 0.05; 1.62 / 1.66 at 0.10; 1.21 / 1.25 at 0.15; 0.91 / 0.95 at 0.20; 0.68 / 0.72 at 0.25; 0.49 / 0.53 at 0.30; 0.33 / 0.37 at 0.35; 0.19 / 0.22 at 0.40; 0.06 / 0.09 at 0.45; 0.00 / 0.03 at 0.4764, each the passing end of a bracket of width 1/100 with the refusal one step above it. Deep in the region the expansion tolerates a non-Wilson content of order one per plaquette; the trade is explicit, each step deeper buying budget and costing one more renormalisation step over which the content must not grow.

The content the proof consumes. A sup-norm content does not pair with this budget: the bond b_C = e^{δ_C} − 1 sits inside the Haar integral that produces each polymer's weight, and the bound |∫ G b_C| ≤ ‖b_C‖_∞ ∫|G| discards the cancellation in ∫G that is the exact non-abelian pricing of Steps 19–21. The mechanism that keeps it: expand each bond in the Peter–Weyl basis of the links of C, b_C = Σ_ρ b̂_C(ρ) φ_ρ; each mode's Haar integral against the Wilson character product is again an exact integral of a character product, a flux surface in the gas's own alphabet, priced by the gas's own lemmas. Two structural facts follow from link balance (the tensor product of the representations incident at a link contains the trivial one, or the integral vanishes). (b1) At a link of multiplicity two the two incident spins are equal, so on a branch-free component a bond mode changes coefficients only and never representations, when its link content lies on no separating cycle of the component; a mode whose link content lies on a separating cycle creates a wall across that neck, the sides may then differ in spin, and the configuration is priced as a wall with mixed sides, whose factor at the number is at most (2a_{3/2}/a_½)⁵ ≈ 10⁻¹¹. (b2) Bond-created flux on plaquettes the Wilson expansion left bare attaches to a spin-½ surface at links of multiplicity three or more at spin 1 (½ ⊗ ½ ⊗ k ∋ 0 forces k ∈ {0, 1}), as the gas's walls and patches; at a multiplicity-four link a created plaquette at spin 2 is admitted; two or more created plaquettes on one attachment link admit spin ½, and a created spin-½ sheet is a surface of the gas with the bond's coefficient in a_½'s place; created flux with no Wilson surface under it survives only when C contains a closed plaquette set, |C| ≥ 6. So the full gas at the exit scale is the flux-surface gas with its alphabet, each plaquette's coefficient drawn from Wilson's a_j and from the bonds' modes: no new lemma is needed for the shapes, only for the coefficients. In units of the Wilson coefficient a mode stands in for or modifies, the relative content of a bond is r_C := Σ_{ρ≠0} |b̂_C(ρ)| · cg(ρ) / Π_{p created by ρ} (a_{k_p} d_{k_p}), cg the channel multiplicity, and c_rel(p) := Σ_{C∋p} r_C e^{α|L(C)|}, c_rel := sup_p c_rel(p). If the Wilson gas at β_c satisfies the inequality with a(X) = α|L(X)| + ε|X|, if c_rel ≤ ε, and if the decorated surfaces' topological factors are the undecorated ones', then the full gas satisfies it with a′(Z) = α|L(Z)|: the dressing of a surface S by bond trees is at most Π_{p∈S}(1 + c_rel(p)) ≤ e^{ε|S|}, exactly what the tilt charges, and the induction of Kotecký and Preiss closes. The amplification is a number before anything is believed: a mode that creates spin-½ flux is weighed against 2a_½(β) = 2I₂(β)/I₁(β), from 40 at β = 0.05 to 5.51 at 0.3650, a spin-1 mode against 3a₁ = 3I₃/I₁, from 3200 to 61, and a mode that only modifies an existing plaquette is charged once.

The pricing-comparison lemma, and the exit condition. Every pricing lemma of the gas bounds a Haar integral of a product of characters and intertwiners, with the plaquettes' coefficients standing outside the integral; hence a decorated composite, a Wilson surface carrying bond modes that leave its representations fixed and bond-created walls and patches at its branch links, is priced by the same decomposition the gas prices its own surfaces by, with the bond's coefficient in the place of the Wilson coefficient of the plaquettes the bond created and each modified plaquette's coefficient multiplied by one plus the mode's Clebsch–Gordan share. The proviso of the second reader: a lemma whose statement bounds the integral holds with any coefficients outside; a lemma whose proof used a property of Wilson's a_j holds for the blocked a′_j only when that property is checked, and the properties are positivity, monotonicity in the spin (a′_{j+½} ≤ a′_j), the tail premise a_{j+1} ≤ a_j/8 under which the spin sums converge, and the dressing recursion's monotonicity in the wall coefficient, which holds by its form, every term being non-negative and increasing in it. The exit condition is then a run of the certificate with the blocked action's own coefficients and no tilt: (i) the one-plaquette coefficients a′_j read off the marginal's modes, d_j a′_j = E[χ_j(A)]; (ii) each spin-½ plaquette's coefficient multiplied by 1 + r_mod(p), the sum through p of the bonds' modifying modes, charged once; (iii) the wall and patch coefficient a₁ of the dressing recursion replaced by the larger of a₁ and the bonds' creating share per plaquette, the geometric mean of a bond's coefficient over the plaquettes it creates; (iv) the modes that neither modify a spin-½ plaquette nor create flux priced through the spin sum with the coefficient in place of a_j; with the mixed-side factor of (b1) multiplying the lone-wall and surface-piece activities. The certificate refuses by name a negative entry, a sequence not non-increasing in the spin, and a breach of the tail premise; a pass is a pass under those checks and no more.

The first step, read. At β = 2.2 the one-step blocked coefficients at a fixed exterior (the exact two-face object of Step 24) are outside the gas by the certificate's own word at every exterior read: at the aligned exterior the one-plaquette coefficient is Wilson's at β ≈ 1.85 and the wall floor, 3.84 on the corrected object, is three orders of magnitude above an exit's a₁ ≈ 0.003, so the dressing recursion has no fixed point (the iteration leaves [0, 3]); at a Haar-random exterior the blocked one-plaquette weight has E[χ₁(A)] below zero and is not a positive character series at all. None of this is a surprise and all of it is a measurement: the window must be crossed by several blocking steps whose content decays, and whether it does is the theorem.
The explanation

The one open link of the whole chain is made precise here as a comparison of two numbers at one scale: the budget, which the certified gas supplies as a table, and the content, the multi-plaquette part of the blocked action at the exit scale, which must be read uniformly in the cutoff. The lemma's subtlety is in which content: a supremum norm throws away the very cancellations that made the gas converge to β* rather than to the classical radius, so the content must be read mode by mode in the gas's own character alphabet, where a bond's effect is to modify a coefficient or to create a wall or a patch, each priced by the lemmas already proved. The exit condition is then not a tilt but a run of the same certificate with the blocked coefficients handed to it, which is also what makes it falsifiable at every stage: the first step from the crossover coupling fails it outright, with the reason printed.

Step 24 — What exact finite objects can read: the two-face object, the influence inequalities, the abelian gate, and the two one-loop teeth

The mathematics

The influence inequalities. For a coarse variable A and a block B, let b_{AB} = sup ‖μ_A(·|ω) − μ_A(·|ω′)‖_TV over coarse exteriors differing at B alone, Hypothesis I's coefficient, and for a fine configuration of every link but ℓ let β_{Aℓ} = sup_{U,U′} ‖μ_A(·|ℓ = U) − μ_A(·|ℓ = U′)‖_TV be the fine influence of ℓ on A at that configuration. The mixture inequality, and its direction. Let v be a coarse configuration, v′ the same with B's value changed, ω the fine exterior of the object, ν(·|v) its conditional law, and C_ω(A, B) = sup_{V,V′} ‖p_ω(·|B = V) − p_ω(·|B = V′)‖_TV the interdependence coefficient of the object's own joint law at the exterior ω, beside its tilt quantity Δ_ω(A, B) = sup_{V,V′} osc_U [log p_ω(U|V) − log p_ω(U|V′)] with C_ω ≤ 1 − e^{−Δ_ω}. The explanation

An exact engine on a finite object computes the law of two coarse plaquettes given everything outside them, and the lesson of this step is what such a law can and cannot decide. It can read the integrand of Hypothesis I at one point of the fibre, exactly and in the hypothesis's own currency; it cannot integrate the fibre or take the supremum over it, and the inequalities above place each reading as a lower bound on a quantity whose other side is unseen. The decisive test is the abelian one: a theory with a massless photon passes every fixed-exterior criterion, because pinning the exterior cuts off the infrared, so a reading that passes SU(2) passes U(1) by the same mechanism and decides nothing. The two teeth are the opposite kind of statement: a method whose output is the free field's ratio of one and the non-abelian one-loop coefficient b₀ to one percent, with the abelian theory at zero and charged matter screening, is a method that reads what it claims to read at weak coupling; at the crossover it must be replaced by the theorem's own hypothesis read on the coarse measure, which the remaining steps construct.

Step 25 — The flow as one object: the fibre-to-coarse lemma and its limit, THE ONE FLOW theorem, the Two-Sector Theorem, and the fibre's exact Gaussian rate

DATE: 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-03. STATUS: the lemma PROVED with its two precisions; THE ONE FLOW theorem PROVED as an architecture with every input named and graded; the Two-Sector Theorem PROVED; the fibre's Gaussian rate PROVED on three roads, the third exact in ℤ[√2]; the reflection positivity of the fibre at symmetric coarse data PROVED.
The mathematics

The fibre-to-coarse lemma. In Step 13's setting with a block-local coarse map and versions of the conditional laws defined for every coarse configuration: let ∂y be the fine links outside the block B_y that share a plaquette with a link of B_y (they lie in the 80 blocks at distance one); let p_y(dv_y|ω_∂) be the law of the coarse variable v_y given the links of ∂y, a finite pinned object because the Wilson measure's conditional law of B_y given everything outside depends only on ∂y; let δ_y = sup_{ω,ω′} ‖p_y(·|ω_∂) − p_y(·|ω′_∂)‖_TV be its ergodicity coefficient; and let T_∂(y, y′) be the supremum, over coarse configurations differing only at y′, of the total variation between the fibre laws of ω_∂ given the coarse configuration. Then for y ≠ y′ and δ_y below one, C^λ_j(y, y′) ≤ δ_y T_∂(y, y′)/(1 − δ_y). Proof. By the tower and Markov properties, λ(dv_y|v_{−y}) = ∫ p_y(dv_y|ω_∂) μ̃(dω_∂|v_{−y}) with μ̃ the law of ω_∂ given the coarse configuration off y, itself the mixture μ̃(·|v_{−y}) = ∫ ν_j(dω_∂|w, v_{−y}) λ(dw|v_{−y}). For v, v′ differing only at y′ write c for the total variation between λ(·|v_{−y}) and λ(·|v′_{−y}); Dobrushin's contraction gives c ≤ δ_y ‖μ̃ − μ̃′‖, inserting ∫ ν(·|w, v′_{−y}) λ(dw|v_{−y}) and the triangle inequality gives ‖μ̃ − μ̃′‖ ≤ T_∂ + c, and so c(1 − δ_y) ≤ δ_y T_∂. ∎ The tower step needs block-locality, σ(v_{−y}) ⊆ σ(links outside B_y), which a straddling coarse map, Bałaban's averaged variables included, does not have; at δ_y = 1 the bound is vacuous. Under Hypothesis II(b) applied to indicators of ω_∂, T_∂(y, y′) ≤ min(1, 80K′ρ′^{|y−y′|−1}), so Hypothesis I holds with (κ, α) as soon as δ S/(1 − δ) ≤ α with S(K′, ρ′, κ) = Σ_{r≥1} n(r) min(1, 80K′ρ′^{r−1}) e^{κr}, n(r) = (2r+1)⁴ − (2r−1)⁴: the threshold δ* = 1/(1 + S) is 9.2 × 10⁻⁷ at (K′, −ln ρ′, κ) = (1, 1, 0.5), 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ at (1, 4, 1), 3.1 × 10⁻³ at (1, 8, 1), 4.6 × 10⁻³ at (1, 16, 1), the near shells (80 at r = 1) setting it. Why it does not close the window: δ_y is a supremum over pinned fine data, and for a gauge-covariant coarse link it is of order one at every scale, since pinned boundary data can align the links adjacent to ∂y (an effective field of order β times the number of straddling plaquettes) or rotate them (a gauge transformation of the data at the boundary sites rotates the law of v_y), so p_y(·|ω_∂) is far from Haar and depends strongly on ω_∂ even where the blocked law is near Haar; the blocked measure's small influence at a strongly coupled coarse scale comes from averaging over the fibre's strongly fluctuating boundary layer, which the pinned supremum discards. Every route through a pinned supremum of a gauge-covariant coarse variable is closed by this: the window's difficulty is the averaging over the fibre of gauge-covariant coarse links at O(1) coupling.

THE ONE FLOW theorem. The object is the renormalisation-group flow of the G-gauge theory: the sequence of effective measures A₀ (Wilson's action at the bare β₀), A₁, A₂, … on the coarse fields at scales a, La, L²a, …, each obtained from the last by one exact blocking step, with its fibre law (the finer field given the coarser); its aspects at each scale are the effective coupling β_k, the cone C(β) it lies in, and the clustering constants (K′, ρ′) of its fibre. Let G be a compact simple group and suppose there are cones {C(β) : β ≥ β_s} of effective actions, a drift c(β) and fibre constants (K′, ρ′) such that (F1) Wilson's action at β lies in C(β) for β ≥ β_s; (F2) one exact blocking step maps C(β) into C(β − c(β)) for every β ≥ β_s, with c(β) ≥ c_min above zero and c(β) tending to the asymptotic-freedom rate as β → ∞, and its fibre satisfies Hypothesis II with (K′, ρ′) uniformly; (F3) C(β_s) lies inside a strong-coupling region where a certified expansion gives Hypothesis I (Step 22's certificate in its coefficient-supplied mode for SU(2); Osterwalder and Seiler's region for every G). Then for every bare β₀ the flow enters C(β_s) after k* ≤ (β₀ − β_s)/c_min steps; because c(β) has the asymptotic-freedom rate, along the asymptotically free sequence the exit scale L^{k*}a converges to a fixed physical length; Hypotheses I and II then hold there uniformly in the cutoff, and Steps 13 and 15 give every limit point a unique vacuum and a Hamiltonian with no spectrum in (0, m), m above zero. The group dependence sits in one place, the drift: c(β) is positive for every non-abelian G, with b₀ = 11C_A/(48π²) in the program's normalisation, and zero for U(1), so the U(1) flow never reaches the exit, which is the control every valid chain must pass. Hypothesis I is the statement that the flow is in the strong-coupling cone at the exit scale; Hypothesis II is the statement that the fibres cluster, accumulated along the flow; the window is (F2) and (F3) on the bounded interval [β_s, β_x] of couplings, together with Hypothesis II's crossover part.

The Two-Sector Theorem. The averaged fibre covariance is exactly the sum of the per-step averaged fibre covariances (the Scale Lemma). The span of the coarse-observable states reduces the Hilbert space, and Hypothesis I alone gives that coarse sector the gap κ/a_c in every limit point; the full gap needs Hypothesis I together with either (C), the completeness of the coarse sector, proved for the free field, or (F), a fibre-sector bound. Every sub-box averaging map is decimation in its codimension, and the fibre is uniformly massive iff that codimension is at most one: the holonomy coarse map of Step 13 is the line case, and its Gaussian fibre is provably not uniformly massive, its rate falling like L^{−1/2} (κ = 1.718, 1.123, 0.746, 0.512 at L = 2, 4, 8, 16), while the averaging map's rate rises to the alias bound; the reduction must therefore compose with averaging maps. The averaging map's Gaussian fibre is massive by the block constraint alone, the precision on the block-zero-mean subspace being bounded below by the block's first nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue g_L = 2 − 2cos(π/L), uniformly in the volume, the mass and the coarse data, and its exact rate is cosh κ = 2 + 3/(L² − 1), κ_∞ = log(2 + √3). The explanation

This step builds the first exact instrument that reads a conditioned fibre at the crossover coupling: fixing a coarse variable by substitution rather than by a kernel costs nothing in spin and makes the constraint exact, and along a strip the fine fluctuations given the coarse edges decay by a constant factor per cell that is a transfer operator's gap, read exactly at every cap the machine reaches and certified datum by datum by two independent eigenvalue enclosures. The theorem on the gauge orbit says what the exterior can and cannot do to that operator: its eigenvalues are invariants of a smaller group than its singular values, which is why a gauge-invariant reading of the exterior cannot predict the eigenvalue gap and why the quantity a uniform statement should use is the one invariant under the whole residual group. Jentzsch's theorem supplies the one uniform fact available without a value: the exact cell's gap is positive at every exterior and bounded away from zero over the compact space of exteriors. The missing lemma is a structural one, the gap as a function of few invariants of the exterior's holonomy through the cell, and the engines now give its first table.

The explanation

This step reads the Gaussian fibre of the averaging map to the bottom. Its rate is an exact algebraic number at every momentum, a rational law at the corners of the Brillouin zone with the mass entering linearly, and its dominant mode alternates in sign at every block step, so the operator whose gap governs the fibre is the two-step one, a structure the exact engines of Step 28 met independently at disordered exteriors. The whole spectrum at the massless corners is integer and is derived from one factorisation: the aliases the average cannot see keep their fine dispersion, which the Chebyshev polynomial of the block size turns into the integers observed. Which pole leads is not left to a real-line reading but decided by counting roots in a disc exactly. The Perron certificate shows the shape every certified statement of this document takes: an enclosure where the arithmetic can enclose, and a refusal by name where it cannot, with a second instrument supplying what the first refused. The three constants derived at the end close small debts the chain had carried: a posited coefficient, a threshold's origin, and a hinge's confinement reading.

Step 35 — The coarse-point reading: Hypothesis I's row in the SU(2)⁴-per-site form, specified, its first-order law with the product couplings, and read on the fitted coarse action

DATE: 2026-11-03. STATUS: the first-order law PROVED in the form below; the single-link rows READ on the fitted action (the couplings a reading by score matching on a Monte Carlo record, the arithmetic on them exact); the exact first-order bundle row READ, 1.097 at the two-step scale, above one; the bundle row of the exact law at the ordered environment READ as a lower bound by fixed functions, 1.176 ± 0.049 by the sampler's error and ± 0.055 with the fitted couplings' error included, at the two-step scale, ABOVE ONE by 3.2 standard errors — the kill-switch fires in the reduction's own variable as a reading on the fitted action, as the single-link reading fired it by quadrature — and 0.313 ± 0.048 at the three-step scale, below one on couplings known to their own size; the row bounded above, uniformly in the environment, by the Birkhoff–Hopf ceiling 10.77; nothing certified and nothing uniform in the environment.
The mathematics

The object. Hypothesis I of Step 13 in the form Step 14 gives it (the L² row): at a coarse site Y the variable is the bundle V(Y) = (V₀, V₁, V₂, V₃) ∈ SU(2)⁴ of tree-averaged coarse links (the axial-tree transport of each of the n⁴ fine lines of a block to its centre, their sum normalised to the group; gauge covariant, the identity at n = 1, its legs a coarse gauge transformation so that a coarse loop is the chain-map smoothing of the flux with no perimeter self-energy); for two sites and an environment ξ (every other bundle) the pair's maximal correlation is ρ(Y, Y′ | ξ) = sup E[f(V(Y))g(V(Y′)) | ξ] over f, g of zero conditional mean and unit conditional variance; the row entry is R(Y, Y′) = ess sup_ξ ρ(Y, Y′ | ξ) and the hypothesis at the block scale is Σ_{Y′ ≠ Y} R(Y, Y′)e^{κ|Y − Y′|} < 1 for some κ > 0. It is one predicate; the certified strong-coupling row of Step 16 (the decimated measure of the perfect cover) is another, and the single-link row of Step 27 (one coarse link against its 122 neighbours; 1.163904 ± 0.024706 at the ordered environment on the fitted twelve-term action) a third, since the four links of a site are read together and a bundle's zero-mean functions include the products across its links. What each reading can say: by the continuity and positivity of the fitted density, R(Y, Y′) ≥ ρ(Y, Y′ | ξ₀) for the ordered environment ξ₀ entry by entry, so a row sum at or above one at ξ₀ refutes the hypothesis on the fitted action and a row sum below one proves nothing by itself; the ordered environment is the premise of any environment criterion, never its certificate.

The first-order law. Write the fitted coarse action as S = −Σ_ℓ Σ_j t_{ℓ,j} χ_j(U_ℓ)/d_j over the four loop families of a site (plaquettes 6, rectangles 12, chairs 48, parallelograms 16; 120 loop incidences per link) with the normalised characters x, (4x² − 1)/3, 2x³ − x in x = ½ tr U. Lemma (the bundle's first-order correlation). Consider a loop ℓ whose links in the bundle at Y are a₁, …, a_p and whose links in the bundle at Y′ are b₁, …, b_q, every other link of ℓ the identity; its trace is χ_j of the ordered product of those p + q links with their traversal directions. Its contribution to the first-order cross-covariance between the bundles' function spaces is a coupling of strength t_{ℓ,j}/d_j² between the normalised matrix elements of the product P_ℓ = V_{a₁}^{±} ⋯ V_{a_p}^{±} (a function of the bundle at Y of degree p) and those of the product Q_ℓ of the b's (degree q), under the pairing fixed by the orientation: by Schur orthogonality E|D^j_{mn}(U)|² = 1/d_j for a Haar U and the product of Haar elements is Haar, so √d_j D^j_{mn}(P_ℓ) and √d_j D^j_{mn}(Q_ℓ) have unit variance, and χ_j(P_ℓ Q_ℓ^{±}) = Σ_{mn} D_{mn}(P_ℓ)D_{nm}(Q_ℓ^{±}) couples them at t_{ℓ,j}/d_j · (1/d_j). The first-order maximal correlation of the two bundles is the largest singular value of the cross-covariance over all these functions, loops with the same (P_ℓ, Q_ℓ) adding coherently and loops with orthogonal parts adding as separate blocks; different spins are orthogonal at this order. Proof. The zeroth-order covariance of the normalised matrix-element functions of distinct products is the identity where the products are distinct as functions (for two links a, a′ the functions D(V_a), D(V_{a′}) and D(V_aV_{a′}) are mutually orthogonal under Haar; for spin ½ the real part of V_aV_{a′} equals that of V_{a′}V_a while the vector parts differ by the commutator), the first-order cross-covariance is Σ_ℓ t_{ℓ,j}E₀[F G χ_j(U_ℓ)/d_j] with the only nonvanishing terms those where F and G are the matrix elements of the loop's two products, and the maximal correlation of two random vectors with identity covariances is the largest singular value of their cross-covariance. ∎ The single link is the case p = q = 1 for every loop, where ρ₁ = max_j Σ_ℓ |t_{ℓ,j}|/d_j² with every sign aligned, and summed over the neighbours it is (1/4)Σ_{ℓ ∋ c}(|ℓ| − 1)|t_{ℓ,½}| plus the higher spins, Step 27's multiplicity law. For the bundles the plaquettes at a site have p = 2 and q = 1 (the plaquette at Y in the plane (a, ν) holds the links a and ν of Y and the link ν of Y + e_a), so their first-order couplings are isolated entries t/4 between a product of Y and a single link of Y + e_a, one per plane — three orthogonal entries, maximal correlation t/4 and not a coherent sum; the loops with p = q = 1 (the rectangles, chairs and parallelograms through one link of each bundle) populate the single-link block, and loops with two links in each bundle the product-to-product block. The first figures this step carried for the bundle rows were computed by an instrument that entered every p = 2, q = 1 plaquette as two coherent single-link entries, and they are withdrawn: on the plaquette couplings alone the first-order bundle row at a_c = 4a is twenty sites (the eight nearest and the twelve at Y′ = e_μ − e_ν) at t/4 = 0.0321 each, 0.642, the earlier instrument's estimate, not 0.916, and the bundle row is not one and a half times the single-link row.

So at the two-step scale the bundle form's row at the ordered environment lies in [0.85, 2.635] with the estimate at 0.905, below one on every reading but the triangle bound, where the single-link form's row is 1.164 by exact quadrature: the refutation that the single-link reading of Step 27 carried does not transfer to the reduction's own variable; a row below one at one environment proves nothing, the hypothesis being an essential supremum over environments, and whether the exact row there exceeds one is for a sharper upper bound or a richer basis to decide, the typical-environment row and the straddling lemma's bound the roads to the supremum. The ceiling, uniform in the environment (Birkhoff and Hopf's contraction of Hilbert's projective metric, classical). For a pair law p(u, v) = a(u)b(v)e^{h(u,v)}/Z on compact spaces with a, b > 0 and h bounded, the maximal correlation of u and v is at most tanh(Δ/4), Δ = sup over u, u′, v, v′ of h(u,v) + h(u′,v′) − h(u,v′) − h(u′,v): the two conditional kernels have projective diameter at most Δ, a and b cancelling from every cross-ratio, each contracts the projective metric by tanh(Δ/4), and the squared maximal correlation is the second eigenvalue of their composition. For two bundles at any environment, h is the sum over the loops shared by the two bundles of t_{ℓ,j}χ_j(U_ℓ)/d_j, every other term of the action a function of one bundle or of the environment alone, so with the ranges of the normalised characters (2, 4/3, 2) doubled, Δ(Y, Y′) ≤ Σ_shared (4|t_{ℓ,½}| + (8/3)|t_{ℓ,1}| + 4|t_{ℓ,3/2}|) and R(Y, Y′) ≤ tanh(Δ(Y, Y′)/4) entry by entry. On the fitted twelve-term action at 4a each of the eight nearest sites shares 75 loops with the origin, Δ = 3.1985 and tanh(Δ/4) = 0.6638, and the ceiling of the row over the 88 sites sharing a loop is 10.77; the single-link form of the same bound reads 5.59, and on the plaquette-only action the one-loop pair's ceiling is 0.1301 against its exact 0.0327, the factor four of looseness that the free environment shows. At a_c = 8a the coarser record's couplings are known to their own size — the plaquette coupling 0.00571 ± 0.00433 and every other within 1.6 of its error of zero — so a reading there is a reading of one point of the fit's error region: at the central line the exact first-order row is 0.215, the fixed-function reading of the exact law with the spin-½ optimal pair 0.206 ± 0.052 (at its level, the three spin blocks being comparable there), and the environment-uniform first-order bound 0.599, below one, while at the spin-½ couplings' one-sigma upper corner the same bound is 1.18; the three-step scale is reached by no instrument of this work to the precision a verdict needs, the exact ones not reaching it and the fitted one not determining its action. An upper bound below one at any scale would need the second singular value of the exact pair kernel, whose weight e^{S} is not a polynomial, and no instrument of this step computes it. The supremum over environments, attacked by a search (a lower bound of a supremum): the first-order operator at an arbitrary environment is the same Haar-orthogonal matrix with each coordinate choice's coefficient the real part of the numeric product of the environment's loop constants and the basis quaternions, exact at every environment and gauge-invariant; a coordinate ascent over the shared loops' environment links from the ordered environment and from six Haar-random ones finds, at the two-step scale, a best environment 0.7 % above the ordered one for the nearest pair and 1.0 % for the pair e_μ − e_ν, every random start climbing back to within 0.3 % of it, and at the three-step scale the ordered environment a strict local maximum, every random start ending below it; the exact law read at that best environment is 0.0543 ± 0.0017 against the ordered environment's 0.0560 ± 0.0015 — so the ordered environment is the hard case for the first-order correlation within one per cent, as a reading, and nothing is proved about the supremum of the exact law. One statement is a theorem of the first-order operator: each loop's block has a norm independent of the environment, so the first-order row of suprema is at most the triangle sum, 2.635 at the two-step scale and 0.599 at the three-step scale — below one there uniformly in the environment at the fit's central line, and 1.18 at the couplings' one-sigma upper corner — while the exact law's second-order terms, comparable to the first at both scales because the loops are many, are bounded uniformly by nothing sharper than the Birkhoff–Hopf ceiling. The four loop families of these instruments are the fitted action's own, loop for loop: one enumeration, compared with the generated header the fit's sampler compiled, matches it one to one by every loop's unoriented link set, with a bent chair refused; and the census of the loops shared by two bundles, at all eighty-eight coarse offsets that share one, is met by a second enumeration from that header sharing no line with the first. The condition that fails here is the single-site one: by the currency inequality of Step 15, R_j(y, y′)² ≤ C^λ_j(y, y′)C^λ_j(y′, y), and translation covariance, under which a row of C^λ_j and the corresponding column have equal sums, the correlation row is at most Dobrushin's total-variation row, so the reading above refutes Dobrushin's single-site condition and Hypothesis I together with Hypothesis I′, on the fitted action. The criterion of Dobrushin and Shlosman for a finite block V — Σ_{y∈∂V} k_{V,y} < |V|, with k_{V,y} the supremum over boundary conditions of the Wasserstein distance, for the sum metric on the block's configurations, between the block's conditional law and the law with one boundary site changed, per unit of that change (Dobrushin and Shlosman 1985; in the form stated by Shlosman 2025), the single-site condition its |V| = 1 case — is not refuted at this scale by anything computed here, and the pairing of the two directions that serves the single site is not available to it. For a block, the block's law is at least as far from its neighbour's, for the discrete metric on each site, as any site marginal, and a site's total-variation response to one boundary site is at least the square of their maximal correlation, the χ²-contraction of the channel between them, which its total-variation contraction dominates; the correlation itself bounds no one-sided influence from below — the three-point channel with influence p has maximal correlation √p, the reverse influence being one. So Σ_{y∉V} max_{x∈V} ρ(x, y)², with ρ the maximal correlation of the pair law in which the block's other sites are integrated, bounds the boundary sum from below; the first-order table holds those sites at the ordered environment instead, and with it the sum reads 0.015|V| for the 2⁴ block and 0.0088|V| for 3⁴, far below |V|, readings of a different conditioning and not bounds. What the criterion asks at this scale is the block's interior response to its boundary, which no first-order operator gives, and that is the object of the next step. The single-site condition that fails here is, moreover, not the exit's criterion: the exit of this argument is Theorem 8.9's — the surface-gas certificate of Steps 18 and 22 applied to the blocked action, whose exponential clustering is what Theorem 7.1 takes — and the single-site row and the certificate are two sufficient conditions of very different strength, the Wilson action itself failing the row near β ≈ 0.12 while its surface gas is certified to 0.3650 under the four inputs of Step 17. On the fitted two-step-blocked action the plaquette coupling, 0.128 in the certificate's own normalization, lies inside that radius by a factor 2.8, where the one-step action's 0.958 lies outside; this is a reading of a twelve-term fit and not a step — the blocked action's omitted terms are bounded by nothing here, and its long loops, whose activity through a link is seven tenths of the plaquettes', are faces of a second kind. Entered as faces, they change the reading: the six-link loops, each with the two plaquettes it bounds, raise the certificate's sum through a link ten-thousand-fold, from 6·10⁻⁸ for the plaquette gas alone to 6.3·10⁻⁴; and counted exactly — every minimal closed surface of at most six faces of the four shapes through a link, twelve million of them, each counted once, and the surfaces beyond six faces bounded by the closing tree — the whole sum at the allowance 2·10⁻³ is 1.0·10⁻³, half of it, when the surfaces beyond six faces are bounded by the finite bound described below, and 3.1·10⁻³, short of it, with the closing tree's uniform weight. On the fitted twelve-term action the criterion is therefore met with a factor two in the sum, at the scale where the single-site condition fails; ninety-nine and a half per cent of the counted sum lies on surfaces with every link in exactly two faces, where the bound 2^χ ≤ 4 is the classical surface integral, and the census, being a count on the lattice and not a function of the couplings, holds for any action of these four shapes. The margin is a reading of the twelve-term fit and not a step: the loops of eight links, 2,868 of them through a link, which a seventeen-term fit resolves only to within two standard errors of zero, add about a tenth to the weight through a link at their central values, and the closing tree that bounds the surfaces beyond six faces charges every face at every step, so on the fuller fit the criterion in this form fails — while those loops' own closed surfaces, each needing a disc of further faces to close, are small. A certificate for the blocked action itself therefore needs a bound on the surfaces beyond the census that charges each open surface its cost of closing rather than the tree's uniform weight, and such a bound holds in finite form. The closing tree adds a face through the smallest odd link l of a configuration, so the face's odd links are among its links ordered at or after l; if, at each link direction, the sum over the faces f through l of w_f ρ^{|f| − 2k_f}, with k_f the number of the face's links ordered at or after l, is at most one, then every open configuration completes with total weight at most ρ to the size of its boundary — by induction on the depth, adding a face changes the boundary's size by |f| − 2k, and a closed configuration completes with weight one. For the action fitted on two thousand configurations at the two-step scale the sum over plaquettes, six-link loops and eight-link loops is 0.86 at ρ = 0.80 and 0.68 at ρ = 0.85 (0.99 and 0.78 at the fit’s one-standard-error corner), the three lengths contributing 0.34, 0.30, 0.22 and 0.29, 0.23, 0.16: readings of a fit, not bounds. The parts fall slowly with the loop’s length — by 0.88 and 0.75 at ρ = 0.80, by 0.81 and 0.68 at ρ = 0.85 — and they fall slowly for a reason: the clustering of the fine field bounds a blocked coupling by its loop’s diameter, not its length, and the number of loops no wider than one cell grows with the length (96 of the 114 six-link loops through a link, 1,344 of the 2,868 eight-link loops and 5,280 of the 81,540 ten-link loops lie inside one unit cell). The fit resolves exactly such loops: the two eight-link classes it separates from zero are the two inside one cell, and each compact class carries a number of order one times the plaquette coupling to the power of the area the loop spans — the loops the plaquette term generates, which decay in area. If every further length repeated the last measured ratio the sum would be 1.5 at ρ = 0.80, 1.0 at ρ = 0.85 and 0.76 at ρ = 0.90; that is a rule of continuation, not a measurement, and the weight of the ten-link and longer loops is what decides the finite condition at the two-step scale. On the fitted action through its eight-link loops the surface-gas certificate’s inequality holds at α = 0.015 with its left side at 0.56 of the allowance at the sharpest admissible setting of its Peierls parameter (0.65 at the grid’s setting first read), the least ratio over the rate being 0.56 at α = 0.0135 and the inequality holding from about 0.004 to 0.031, three quarters of that left side being a bound on the eight-link tail and not counted weight; it fails by that bound at α = 0.002, at 1.64 of the allowance. The counted part is now charged by a theorem — the certificate’s leaf is the minimal closed sets, every one through six faces of contact rank at most one and so at most 4 at the uniform spin, the first closures that hold a closed part being a surplus — while the tail is charged the constant 4 of the contact-leaf bound that Step 17 shows false from 46 plaquettes on, so that the reading is under a false constant there: at the fit’s one-standard-error corner the same inequality fails, its left side at 1.80 of the allowance at the setting first read, and with the tail charged at the proved all-spin rate, a factor √2 a face and a constant 2, it fails by a factor of about six at the setting read, from the plaquette roots alone. At the rate of the known examples, a factor 1.0107 a face, the centre of the fit passes for every constant below 1.6; with the constant 2 at unit rate it reads 1.016 of the allowance at the sharpest admissible setting, a failure by 1.6 per cent that a deeper exact count could turn; under the constant 1 the centre turns at a growth of 1.098 a face. The closed sets that hold a closed part are the composites of the expansion’s tree, charged by the rate at which the certificate weighs a face — four times the rate proved, a forest neighbour at cost one and a cycle neighbour at cost two — and the centre bears a cost of 6.2 a neighbour at its best rate where the tree asks 3; through six faces no such set costs more than 5/3. The dressing of the longer faces, counted by a proved count with the weights of the plaquette gas assumed, costs the centre 4 to 8 per cent of its left side, and the reading stays within the allowance. A second fit’s centre reads 0.81 of the allowance at its sharpest setting (0.93 at the grid’s), with room for a cost of 3.9 a neighbour and a growth of 1.039 a face, and 0.85 to 0.88 under the dressing; the quarter of the allowance between the two central fits of one action is the fit’s error region, which no reading of the gas moves. The exit at the two-step scale is therefore certified by no reading in hand, and it waits on the object the strong-coupling theorem waits on above 0.3650, a proved bound on the contact leaves that grows no faster than their known examples. A fit made on typical configurations cannot say what the blocked action does on the rare ordered ones, so the blocked measure is read directly: for each coarse link, the mean alignment of the link with the sum of its six staples, as a function of the local order n, that sum’s length over six. Under a plaquette action of coupling t the link’s law given the rest is a von Mises–Fisher law of concentration 6tn, so the alignment reads the coupling at every n; and the second moment of n is 1/6 plus one sixth of the rectangle’s expectation plus four times the chair’s, exactly, for every measure. At the two-step scale, on ten million links, the coupling so read is 0.1311 ± 0.0005 and flat in n from 0.03 to 0.85 (χ² = 27 over 33 bins), the tail of n is within eight per cent of that of a plaquette action of coupling 0.13, ordered links do not cluster, and the spin-one moment exceeds the plaquette law’s by thirteen per cent (5.5 standard errors): the blocked measure there is a weakly coupled plaquette law with a resolved remainder, on ordered data as on typical data. At the one-step scale the same reading gives 1.268 ± 0.001, rising from 1.19 to 1.34 as n rises, with ordered links clustering: the blocked law stiffens on ordered data one step below, and not at the two-step scale. At the three-step scale every reading is zero within its error. These are Monte Carlo readings of means over environments; none is a supremum, and none bounds the blocked action. The exit at the two-step scale therefore rests on two things no reading supplies: the weight of the longer loops in the finite condition, and a bound on the blocked action as a function on every coarse configuration — which, by the classical theory of block-averaged measures, follows from the clustering of the fine field constrained to the coarse one, uniformly in the coarse configuration. With that bound and the longer loops’ weight, the census and the finite condition decide: the objects of the next step.
The explanation

The question is whether the reduction's own variable, four links per coarse site read together, makes the contraction hypothesis easier or harder to satisfy than the single-link reading of Step 27, which refuted it at the two-step scale. The first-order law answers in structure: a loop couples the product of its links in one bundle to the product of its links in the other, so the plaquettes at a site, which hold two links of one bundle and one of the next, are isolated couplings of strength t/4 and do not add coherently across the site's links, while the longer loops through one link of each bundle add as in the single-link form. The first figures written for the bundle row counted the plaquettes twice and coherently; they are withdrawn and the corrected instruments' readings replace them. What stands is the single-link row, the sampler's known answers against the exact quadrature, and the structure: at the two-step scale the plaquette couplings alone give a first-order bundle row of 0.65 over twenty sites, the longer loops raise the exact first-order row to 1.097, above one (the first reading's estimate 0.91 was wrong in its orthogonality; the rigorous first-order bound 2.64 stands above it), and the exact law's row, read on the first-order optimal functions fixed before any sample, is 1.176 ± 0.055 with the fit's error included, above one by 3.2 standard errors — the two-step scale, which the single-link reading had closed, is closed in the reduction's own variable too, on the fitted action, at the ordered environment; the three-step scale's row reads 0.31 ± 0.05 there, below one, on couplings a Monte Carlo fit knows only to their own size and no exact instrument of this work reaches: the instruments that certify reach the scales where the one-step contraction fails, and the scale where it holds is reached by a fit alone — the gap between reach and contraction, stated as readings, is the wall of the one-step form of the hypothesis. The reading is exact arithmetic on a fitted action and is not a certificate: the hypothesis is about an essential supremum over environments, and only a refutation can be read at one environment.
